Which part is the book, and which part is ours

الكِتَابFrom the book Reproduced from the printed matn: the Arabic of every narration, the narrator, the source, the repetition counts, the chapter and section titles, and the author's own footnote glosses.
الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction The «قُلْ» strip. The wording is the author's, copied out of his text character for character; deciding which span to lift out is ours.
✎Added by us Everything else: all English translation and transliteration, the word-by-word and line-by-line breakdowns, Establishes, and every Simple Explanation, Word Bank, Deeper Lesson, Quick Check, Activity, flashcard and exercise.

Rule of thumb: the Arabic is the book, the English is ours. Press Book only at the bottom right to strip everything we added and read the matn alone.

How this workbook is arranged

  • Three parts across the top: the Virtues, then the Adhkār (chapters 5–74), then the Ādāb (chapters 75–142).
  • Sections in the row beneath — the book's own thirty section headings.
  • Chapters as chips inside each section, or ☰ for the full index.
  • Four tabs on every narration: Translation, Transliteration, Word by Word, Line by Line.
  • The Arabic is reproduced exactly as the book prints it, tanwīn and all. Verify readings and rulings with a qualified teacher.

Man salaka ṭarīqan
Anyone at all who sets out on a road; the reward is tied to the setting out.
سَلَكَ — root س ل ك. Salaka means to walk a road, not merely to want one. The praise attaches to the walking.
يَلْتَمِسُ فِيهِ عِلْماً
yaltamisu fīhi ʿilman
His purpose on that road is knowledge, not something else he stumbles into.
يَلْتَمِسُ — root ل م س. The book glosses it: he went along a road while seeking. Intention, not accident.
سَهَّلَ اللَّهُ لَهُ بِهِ طَرِيقاً إِلَى الجَنَّةِ
sahhala-llāhu lahu bihi ṭarīqan ilā-l-jannah
Allāh answers a road with a road: the effort here is met with ease there.
سَهَّلَ — root س ه ل. Form II, 'to make smooth'. The road to Paradise is not removed, it is made easy.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

The Road That Rewards Every Step

Think about levelling up in a game. You grind through the early stages, put in the hours, and the next area unlocks. The Prophet ﷺ is describing something way bigger and way more generous: every bit of effort you spend learning your deen, Allah Himself clears and smooths the road to Jannah for you.

And look closely at the wording — it isn't "whoever becomes a scholar," it's "whoever travels a path seeking knowledge." The reward is attached to the journey, not just the finish line. So "a path" includes the small, unglamorous stuff: opening the Qur'an app on the bus, sitting in a halaqah, googling a real question about wudu, walking to a class. Each of those is a step, and each step is being counted.

That completely changes how a hard study day feels. You don't have to wait until you've "finished" learning to earn something — you're being rewarded the whole way there, even on the slow days.

🌱 A gentle check-upNext time studying feels like a grind and you're tempted to quit, remember Who is walking ahead of you, smoothing the road. The effort itself is the worship.
The Reward Is in the Journey

This hadith attaches the reward not to reaching some final rank, but to the act of seeking itself: whoever sets out on a path to gain beneficial knowledge finds that Allah eases their way to Paradise.

"A path" is meant broadly — studying, attending a lesson, travelling to a teacher, or simply making the effort to learn. Every genuine step toward understanding the religion is honoured, so the effort of study is itself a form of worship, and never wasted.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: which small step toward learning could you take today, knowing the effort itself is rewarded?

💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
The reward is tied to the journey, not just the destination. Every step taken toward learning — opening a book, the walk to a class, even the search for a teacher — is itself counted as a step toward Paradise. This reframes the effort of study as worship, so no day of sincere seeking is ever wasted.
🌱 Word root
سَلَكَ · salaka
From س-ل-ك — to travel, to take a path. Taking the physical and intellectual road of learning is itself a road Allāh smooths toward Paradise. Yaltamis (يَلْتَمِس) = he seeks out, gropes for.

The VIP Gift from Allah

People chase all kinds of things they think will make them happy — money, followers, the newest phone, being the best at a sport. So it's worth pausing on what Allah calls a sign that He wants good for someone. It isn't a lottery win. It's a VIP gift: the desire and the ability to actually understand Islam. In Arabic, that deep understanding is called fiqh.

Here's the difference that changes everything:

  • Memorising facts — knowing Muslims pray five times a day, knowing the names of the prayers. Good, and necessary — but it's only step one.
  • Real fiqh — knowing why we pray, feeling the calm it drops into your chest, and seeing how it quietly connects you to Allah through the day.

So those little lightbulb moments — "Ohhh, that's why Allah tells us to be patient," or "Now I finally get what this surah means" — aren't random. According to this hadith, they're a sign Allah is showing you love and wishing good for you.

🌱 A gentle check-upEver feel bored or annoyed by learning your deen? Because the love of it is a gift, treat that flat feeling as a signal — make du'a and ask Allah to soften your heart and bring the curiosity back.
Understanding as a Sign of Good

The Prophet ﷺ described being granted fiqh — a sound, deep understanding of the religion — as a sign that Allah intends good for a person. It is among the greatest gifts, greater than wealth or status.

True understanding is more than memorising rulings; it is grasping their wisdom and feeling their effect on the heart. A sincere love of learning, and a desire to understand, are therefore blessings to be thankful for.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: thank Allah for any love of learning you have — and if it fades, ask Him to restore it.

Being granted real fiqh — depth of understanding, not just memorised facts — is named here as a sign that Allāh wills good for you. That makes the love of learning a gift to be grateful for.

The Deeds That Keep Working the Night Shift

Imagine you make something once — a helpful video, a useful post, a tool — and it keeps helping people for years. You're asleep, you're busy living your life, but it's still out there doing good on its own. Allah gives believers three deeds that work exactly like that, except the reward keeps flowing in even after you've died and can't add anything more.

The three are: ongoing charity (a water well, a tree that keeps fruiting, something beneficial you set up or share), knowledge people keep using (you taught someone even one surah, they teach it to someone else, and the chain keeps going), and a righteous child who keeps making du'a for you after you're gone.

The takeaway is a life strategy, not just a nice fact: start planting these now, while you're young. A small thing that keeps giving quietly beats a big one-off splash that ends the moment it happens.

🌱 A gentle check-upWhat's one small thing you could set up this month — a shared benefit, something you teach, a habit of du'a — that would keep earning for you long after you've forgotten about it?
Deeds That Continue After Death

When a person dies, their record of deeds is sealed — with three exceptions that keep earning reward: an ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge that others continue to use, and a righteous child who prays for them.

These are investments whose benefit outlives us. The hadith encourages us to establish such lasting good while we are able.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: what lasting good could you begin now that would keep benefiting others later?

His company is the highest company there is.
السَّفَرَةِ — root س ف ر. The book glosses these three words: as-safarah are the angels, al-kirām those honoured with Allāh, al-bararah those obedient to Him.

The one for whom reciting is still uphill, who keeps returning to it anyway.

✎Added by us

“Recite the Qurʾān, for it will come on the Day of Resurrection as an intercessor for its companions.”

Iqraʾū-l-Qurʾāna; fa innahu yaʾtī yawma-l-qiyāmati shafīʿan li-aṣḥābih

Iqraʾū-l-Qurʾān
A direct command in the plural: all of you, recite.
اقْرَؤُوا — root ق ر أ. Qaraʾa is to read aloud and to recite. The Qurʾān takes its name from this root.
فَإِنَّهُ يَأْتِي يَوْمَ القِيَامَةِ

What you recite now arrives with you later, as something present.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

How to Land on the 'Best' List

Everyone wants to be the best at something — top of the class, best player on the team, the one with the most followers. Those titles are real, but they fade: records get broken, trends move on. The Prophet ﷺ just handed you the cheat code for the one leaderboard that never resets: learn the Qur'an, and pass it on.

And don't let the word "teach" intimidate you. It doesn't mean you need an ijāzah, a certificate, or a classroom full of students. Teaching one ayah to a younger sibling counts. Helping a friend fix a word in their recitation counts. Sharing what a verse means with someone counts. Do any of that and you've already stepped inside this hadith.

Notice too how "best" is measured here — not the most eloquent reciter, not the richest, not the most famous, but the one who both learns it and gives it away. Knowledge in Islam isn't meant to be hoarded; it grows when you hand it on.

🌱 A gentle check-upWho's one person — a sibling, a friend, a younger kid at the masjid — you could teach even a single line or one meaning to this week?
Learning and Teaching the Qur'an

The Prophet ﷺ named the best of people as those who learn the Qur'an and teach it. Both halves matter: receiving knowledge, and passing it on.

Teaching need not be formal. Sharing a single verse, its meaning, or a correction with another person is part of this virtue. Knowledge in Islam is meant to be spread, not kept.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: what have you learned that you could share with someone this week?

Notice the measure of "best": not the most eloquent or wealthy, but the one who both learns and gives. Even teaching one verse to one person places you in this hadith.

مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ القُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُThose who learn the Qurʾān and teach it.
When Struggling Gets You MORE Reward

In school, struggling usually costs you — you read slower, you score lower, you feel behind. With the Qur'an, Allah completely flips the rules. The fluent memoriser who glides through it is honoured, kept in the company of the noble angels. But then the Prophet ﷺ says something amazing about the person for whom it's hard: the one who stumbles, repeats the word, whose tongue trips up — and keeps going anyway — earns two rewards. One for the recitation, and a second one just for the struggle.

Read that again, because it's easy to miss how kind it is. Your difficulty isn't a penalty; it's literally being counted as extra reward. So the person who reads slowly and messily but refuses to give up may walk away with more than the one it comes easy to.

This is Allah removing every excuse to stay away from His Book. "I'm bad at it" was never a reason to stop — it turns out to be a reason your effort is worth double.

🌱 A gentle check-upIf you've ever felt embarrassed about your recitation and let it keep you from opening the Qur'an, let today be the day that stops. Every clumsy, effortful attempt is being rewarded twice.
Two Rewards for the One Who Strives

The one who recites the Qur'an fluently is in the company of the noble angels. The one who finds it difficult, yet perseveres, receives two rewards — one for the recitation and one for the effort.

This is a mercy for every learner: difficulty in reading is not a shortcoming but a source of added reward. It leaves no excuse to abandon the Qur'an.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: if recitation is hard for you, take encouragement — your effort is doubly rewarded.

A gift for the struggling reader: the fluent memoriser keeps the company of angels, yet the one who stumbles and perseveres earns two rewards — one for the recitation, one for the difficulty. Never let "I'm not good at it" keep you from the Qurʾān.
⭐ Two kinds of reciter, both rewarded
The fluent memoriser is ranked with the angels; the one who struggles through it earns two rewards — one for reciting and one for the effort. Difficulty in learning the Qurʾān is never wasted.
✅ Quick checkHow many rewards does the one who struggles with recitation receive?
أَجْرَانِTwo rewards — one for reciting, one for the effort.
A Friend Who Shows Up on Your Hardest Day

Picture the Day of Judgment — the most stressful day that will ever exist. Everyone is worried only about themselves; even the prophets are focused on their own affair. And in the middle of all that, the Qur'an stands up and speaks on your behalf, asking Allah to let you through. An intercessor — on the day you'll need one most.

But there's a condition tucked into one word: it intercedes for its "companions." A companion isn't someone who owns a beautiful mushaf that sits on a shelf collecting dust. It's someone who actually spends time with it — reads a bit regularly, keeps coming back, the way you keep up with a close friend through small, consistent contact.

That's the encouraging part: you don't build this friendship with one giant effort. You build it with a little, often — a page here, a few ayat there — until the Qur'an knows you well enough to stand up for you.

🌱 A gentle check-upBased on the last week, would the Qur'an recognise you as a companion? If not, the fix is tiny and doable — a few minutes a day is exactly how the friendship gets built.
The Qur'an as Intercessor

The Prophet ﷺ told us to recite the Qur'an, for on the Day of Resurrection it will intercede for those who kept its company.

Its "companions" are those who maintain a regular relationship with it through recitation — not occasional, but consistent. That bond is built gradually, a little at a time.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: how might you keep a small, steady portion of Qur'an in your day?

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

Airplane Mode for the Heart

You know when your phone is on airplane mode? The screen's on, it looks fine, but nothing is actually getting through — no messages, no connection. A heart without dhikr is a bit like that: technically alive, but cut off from the source. The Prophet ﷺ put it even more strongly — he said the gap between the one who remembers Allah and the one who doesn't is like the gap between the living and the dead.

That's not a small comparison. It means dhikr isn't a bonus feature for "extra religious" people — it's the signal that keeps the heart switched on and connected in the first place. When you feel spiritually flat, numb, or distant, it's often not that something dramatic is wrong — the connection just went quiet.

And the fix is genuinely simple, which is the mercy in it. A quiet subḥān Allāh, an alḥamdu lillāh, a little istighfār — that's you turning the signal back on.

🌱 A gentle check-upWhen your heart feels heavy or switched-off, don't wait for some big spiritual moment. Reconnect with something small and immediate — a line of dhikr you already know by heart.
Dhikr and the Living Heart

The Prophet ﷺ compared the one who remembers Allah with the one who does not to the living and the dead. Remembrance is what keeps the heart spiritually alive.

When the heart feels heavy or distant, the remedy is often simply to return to the remembrance of Allah — even a few words of dhikr can revive it.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: when your heart feels distant, return to a short, familiar dhikr.

💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Dhikr is presented not as an optional extra but as the very pulse of a living heart. The remedy for a heavy, distracted heart is rarely complicated — it is to start the tongue and mind moving in His remembrance again.
✅ Quick checkThe one who remembers Allah and the one who doesn't are compared to what?
الحَيِّ وَالمَيِّتِThe living and the dead.
Allah Meets You at Your Expectations

This hadith holds two ideas that can genuinely reshape your relationship with Allah. The first is striking: Allah says, "I am as My servant thinks of Me." In other words, the assumptions you carry about Allah actually shape what you experience. Approach Him expecting mercy, expecting that He hears you and will respond, and you're opening the door to exactly that. Never let shaytan talk you into believing He's just waiting to catch you out.

The second idea is about how remembrance gets paid back — and always with interest. Remember Allah quietly, on your own, and He remembers you in return. Remember Him out loud, among people, and He mentions you in a gathering far better than yours — the angels. Whatever you give, what comes back is greater.

Put together, they're an invitation: come to Allah hopeful, and keep His name on your tongue — because both the hope and the remembrance are met by Him with something bigger.

🌱 A gentle check-upBe honest — when you mess up, what's your gut assumption about Allah: that He's furious and done with you, or that He's near and ready to forgive? Choose the one He told you to choose.
Think Well of Allah

In this sacred hadith, Allah says He is as His servant expects Him to be, and that He is with the one who remembers Him. Whoever remembers Allah privately, Allah remembers within Himself; whoever remembers Him among others, Allah mentions among a better assembly.

Two lessons follow: hold a good opinion of Allah, expecting His mercy; and know that remembrance is always answered with something greater.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: what is your assumption about Allah when you turn to Him — and does it match His promise?

Two principles in one ḥadīth. First: think well of Allāh — expect His mercy and response. Second: remembrance is reciprocated and upgraded — remember Him privately and He remembers you; remember Him before people and He mentions you in a gathering "better than it."
💡 "I am as My servant thinks of Me"
This ḥadīth qudsī invites you to hold a good opinion of Allāh — to expect His mercy and acceptance. And remembrance is reciprocal: remember Him quietly, He remembers you; remember Him among people, He mentions you among a better assembly (the angels).
✅ Quick checkComplete: “I am as My servant ___ of Me.”

The Quiet Ones Who Are Secretly Winning

In every race there are people who pull ahead of the pack. So when the Prophet ﷺ said "the mufarridūn have gone ahead," the Companions immediately wanted to know — who are these frontrunners racing ahead to Allah? The answer probably surprised them: not necessarily the biggest scholars, the wealthiest, or the most famous, but simply the men and women who remember Allah a great deal.

Here's why that's such good news. This is the one kind of "getting ahead" with no entry requirements. You don't need money, status, a title, or even much free time. Dhikr lives in the cracks of your day — on the bus, standing in a queue, walking between classes, washing the dishes. While everyone else is scrolling, you can quietly be climbing a ranking that actually matters.

And notice the Prophet ﷺ named both men and women — this lane to the front is wide open to absolutely everyone.

🌱 A gentle check-upPick one "dead" moment in your daily routine — a commute, a wait, a chore — and make it your dhikr slot for the week. That's you sprinting ahead while it looks like you're just standing around.
Those Foremost in Remembrance

The Prophet ﷺ said the mufarridūn have gone ahead, and explained them as the men and women who remember Allah abundantly.

This rank is open to everyone, regardless of status or circumstance. Remembrance can fill the ordinary moments of the day, making it one of the most accessible ways to draw near to Allah.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: which ordinary moments of your day could you fill with remembrance?

The Best Group Chat in Existence

You know how the energy shifts when you're with the right people doing something that actually matters — there's a calm, a focus, a good feeling you can't quite manufacture alone? Now turn that up to a level only Allah can give. The Prophet ﷺ described a gathering so blessed that four things pour down on it at once: tranquillity settles over everyone, mercy wraps around them like a blanket, the angels literally circle the room, and Allah mentions those people by name to the angels in His presence.

And what earns all of that? Not a huge event, not a famous speaker, not a big budget — just a few people sitting together to read and understand the Qur'an. A couple of friends and a mushaf. That's the whole requirement.

It reframes something we usually treat as optional. Studying your deen alone is good and rewarded — but this hadith is Allah basically saying, "do it together and watch Me pour on the blessings." Community isn't a nice extra in learning; it's where some of the biggest gifts land.

🌱 A gentle check-upWho could you pull into a tiny circle this week — even one friend, one page of Qur'an, fifteen minutes? You'd be building the exact gathering this hadith is describing.
Gatherings of Qur'an and Remembrance

Whenever people gather in a house of Allah to recite and study His Book together, four blessings descend: tranquillity, mercy, the encircling of angels, and Allah's mention of them among those near Him.

This highlights the special value of learning in company. What is gained in such gatherings goes far beyond information.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: could you join or form a small circle to read and study the Qur'an together?

A Bodyguard for Your Private Moments

Here's something quietly beautiful about Islam: it doesn't switch off at the bathroom door. Even in the most ordinary, private, unglamorous moment of your day, there's a du'a — because the Prophet ﷺ taught that the privy is a place where the shayāṭīn (devils) gather, and it's a spot where you're exposed and off-guard.

So saying "Allāhumma innī aʿūdhu bika mina-l-khubuthi wa-l-khabāʾith" before you step in is like switching on a bodyguard for a vulnerable moment. But zoom out and there's a bigger lesson being trained into you: begin every exposed, ordinary moment by turning to Allah. If even the bathroom has its remembrance, then no corner of your day is left "off-grid" from Him.

That's really the heart of this whole workbook — taking the automatic, autopilot parts of daily life and threading them with the remembrance of Allah, until an ordinary day quietly becomes worship.

🌱 A gentle check-upLearn these few words by heart this week and say them every single time, until it's automatic. Turning a daily habit into a moment of remembrance is exactly the goal you're working toward here.
Seeking Refuge Before Entering

The Prophet ﷺ taught this supplication upon entering the place of relieving oneself, seeking Allah's protection from the devils present there.

The wider principle is to begin even our most ordinary and private moments with the remembrance of Allah, so that no part of the day is left outside His protection.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: which everyday moment could you begin with the remembrance of Allah?

Ghufrānak
One word, asking Allāh for His forgiveness on the way out.
غُفْرَانَكَ — root غ ف ر. The book reads it as: O Allāh, forgive me. Grammatically it is the object of an unspoken 'I ask You for'.

رَوَاهُ أَحْمَدُReported by Aḥmad

Sorry — Even for the Small Stuff

Slightly surprising: the first thing the Prophet ﷺ said after using the bathroom was to ask Allah for forgiveness. You didn't sin in there — so why? Scholars explain it two ways, and both are beautiful. One: you just spent a few minutes unable to properly remember Allah, so you gently ask pardon for the gap. Two: it's humility — Allah gave your body an easy way to get rid of what would harm it, and turning to His forgiveness is a way of acknowledging you can never thank Him enough.

Either way, the takeaway is big for anyone building habits: your relationship with Allah isn't only for the "big" moments in the masjid. It threads through the most ordinary — even slightly gross — parts of your day. One word, ghufrānak, keeps the line open.

🌱 A gentle check-upIt's literally one word. Memorise it today and say it every time you leave the bathroom — an effortless, constant top-up of your connection with Allah.
Seeking Forgiveness on Leaving

On leaving the place of relieving oneself, the Prophet ﷺ would say a single word: ghufrānak — "I ask Your forgiveness." Scholars mention two reasons: seeking pardon for the period one could not remember Allah, and humility before Allah's favour in easing the removal of harm from the body.

The lesson is that remembrance and humility can accompany even our most ordinary moments.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: a single word can keep even a routine moment connected to Allah — will you make it a habit?

Why seek forgiveness after simply leaving the bathroom? The scholars mention two gentle reasons: asking pardon for the time one could not remember Allah while relieving oneself, and humility before Allah’s favour in making the removal of harm from the body so easy. Either way, it trains the heart to return to Allah even after the most ordinary moments.

A single word meaning “I ask for Your forgiveness, O Allah.” It is one of the easiest adhkār to memorise — ideal for building the habit of remembering Allah around your daily routine.

Eight Doors, One Sentence

Picture Jannah with eight enormous gates. Now imagine a daily action so beloved to Allah that doing it right unlocks all eight at once — and you get to walk in through whichever you like. That's exactly what the Prophet ﷺ promised the one who makes wudu properly and then simply testifies: there is no god but Allah alone, and Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and messenger.

Think about how ordinary wudu is — you do it several times a day, half on autopilot. This hadith says: don't rush off the second you're done. Add ten seconds of these words, said with presence, and you've just attached an unreal reward to a totally routine act.

🌱 A gentle check-upFor one week, don't leave the sink in silence. Say the shahādah after every wudu and picture those eight gates opening.
The Testimony After Wudu

The Prophet ﷺ taught that whoever performs wudu well and then bears witness to the oneness of Allah and the messengership of Muhammad ﷺ will have the eight gates of Paradise opened for him, to enter by whichever he wishes.

A brief, sincere testimony transforms a routine act of purification into a means of great reward.

Clean Outside, Clean Inside

Wudu washes your hands, face, arms, and feet — the outside. This short add-on du'a asks Allah to sort out the inside too: make me one of the tawwābīn (people who keep coming back to Allah whenever they slip) and the mutaṭahhirīn (people who stay clean — physically, and clean of sin).

It's a genius pairing. Right as the water finishes cleaning your skin, you're asking for your heart to be cleaned as well. Nobody's perfect — the point was never to stop slipping entirely, it's to keep turning back.

🌱 A gentle check-upRepentance isn't a one-time event. Which small habit could you "turn back" from this week — and pair it with this du'a after wudu?
Inner and Outer Purity

This addition, reported by at-Tirmidhī, pairs the outward purity of wudu with a request for inner purity: to be among those who constantly repent (at-tawwābīn) and those who keep themselves pure (al-mutaṭahhirīn).

Purification of the body becomes a reminder to seek purification of the heart.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: how might outward cleansing prompt you toward inner cleansing?

أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ

The first testimony, with the oneness spelled out twice over.
شَرِيكَ — root ش ر ك. Sharīk is a partner with a share in something. Denying it is the heart of tawḥīd.

The reward for those words: forgiveness.

(general note) — dhikr on hearing the adhānWhat is prescribed of dhikr upon hearing the adhān is the following: 1 - He says as the muʾadhdhin says, except in the two ḥayʿalah phrases (“Come to prayer”, “Come to success”), where he says: «There is no power and no strength except by Allāh». 2 - When the muʾadhdhin finishes the two testimonies, he says: «I bear witness that there is no god but Allāh alone, having no partner, and that Muḥammad is His slave and His Messenger. I am content with Allāh as Lord, with Muḥammad as Messenger, and with Islam as religion». 3 - When he has finished the adhān he says: «O Allāh, send prayers and peace upon our Prophet Muḥammad». 4 - After the prayer upon the Prophet ﷺ he says: «O Allāh, Lord of this perfect call and of the prayer to be established, grant Muḥammad al-wasīlah and al-faḍīlah, and raise him to the praiseworthy station which You have promised him».

رَوَاهُ البُخَارِيُّReported by al-Bukhārī

Don’t Just Hear It — Answer It

Most people treat the adhān as background noise. The Prophet ﷺ taught something better: echo it back, phrase by phrase. It’s like a call-and-response — the muezzin calls, you answer, and you’re rewarded for every line. There’s one twist: when he calls “come to prayer” and “come to success,” you don’t just repeat it, you say lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh — “I’ve got no power to actually get up and do this except with Allah’s help.”

That little swap is honest. Answering the call to prayer is only possible through Allah, so you say so.

🌱 A gentle check-upNext adhān, don’t scroll through it. Repeat each line, and answer the two “come to…” calls with the ḥawqala.
Responding to the Adhān

The Prophet ﷺ taught that when you hear the muezzin, you repeat what he says. At “ḥayya ʿala-ṣ-ṣalāh” and “ḥayya ʿala-l-falāḥ,” you instead say lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh, acknowledging that answering the call is only possible by Allah’s enabling.

What could be idle listening becomes an act of worship rewarded phrase by phrase.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: could you treat the adhān as an invitation to respond rather than mere sound?
لَا حَوْلَlā ḥawlathere is no mightphraseح-و-ل
وَلَا قُوَّةَwa lā quwwatanor powerphraseق-و-ي
إِلَّا بِاللَّهِillā billāhexcept with Allahphraseأ-ل-ه
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Repeating after the muezzin turns you from a bystander into a participant in the call — every phrase you echo is rewarded. And at «come to prayer / come to success» you answer with lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh, admitting you have no power to answer that call except by Allah’s help.
✅ Quick checkWhat do you say in place of «ḥayya ʿala-ṣ-ṣalāh»?
لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ“Lā ḥawla wa lā quwwata illā billāh.”
A Duʿāʾ That Unlocks His Intercession

Right after the adhān finishes, there’s a short duʿāʾ asking Allah to give the Prophet ﷺ al-wasīlah — the single highest rank in Paradise — and the “praised station.” Here’s the incredible part: whoever sincerely asks Allah to honour the Prophet ﷺ like this, the Prophet’s ﷺ intercession on Judgement Day becomes due for them.

You ask Allah to elevate the one you love — and in return, he speaks up for you on the day you’ll need it most. Thirty seconds after every adhān.

🌱 A gentle check-upMemorise the wasīlah duʿāʾ this week. Say it after every adhān and remember what it earns you.
The Wasīlah Supplication

After the adhān, the Prophet ﷺ taught a supplication asking Allah to grant him al-wasīlah (the highest station in Paradise) and the praised station. Whoever says it, the Prophet’s ﷺ intercession becomes due for him on the Day of Resurrection.

A brief, sincere duʿāʾ for the Prophet ﷺ carries a great personal reward.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: will you make this short duʿāʾ a fixed habit after each call to prayer?

⭐ Ask, and his intercession is yours
After the adhān, send ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ, then say the wasīlah duʿāʾ. Whoever does so, the Prophet’s ﷺ intercession on the Day of Judgement becomes due for him.
💡 Two easy wins
The window between the adhān and the iqāmah is a time when duʿāʾ is not turned back — so after asking for al-wasīlah, make a little duʿāʾ of your own before you stand to pray.

Chapter 9 — Entering the Masjid and Leaving It
الأَذْكَارُ — اِحْفَظْ وَاعْمَلْ

Workbook — what is said on entering and on leaving the masjid.

About this itemمَتَى وَكَيْف · When & how
Entering
Step in with the right foot, send ṣalāh on the Prophet ﷺ, then say the duʿāʾ of mercy
Leaving
Step out with the left foot, then ask Allah of His bounty
Why the pairing
Inside you seek mercy; outside you go to seek provision
Source
رَوَاهُ مُسْلِم · Muslim
١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا دَخَلَ أَحَدُكُمُ المَسْجِدَ فَلْيَقُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ. وَإِذَا خَرَجَ فَلْيَقُلِ: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ»

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْSay on entering the masjid. On leaving, say the second duʿāʾ in this entry: اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ (Allāhumma innī asʾaluka min faḍlik).
اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ
✎Added by us

“When one of you enters the masjid, let him say: ‘O Allāh, open for me the gates of Your mercy.’ And when he leaves, let him say: ‘O Allāh, I ask You of Your bounty.’”

Idhā dakhala aḥadukumu-l-masjida fal-yaquli
On the way in, there is something to say before anything else.
فَلْيَقُلِ — root ق و ل. The lam on fal-yaqul is a command: let him say it. It is an instruction, not a suggestion.
اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ
Allāhumma-ftaḥ lī abwāba raḥmatik
Going in, you ask for mercy, because the masjid is where mercy is sought.
أَبْوَابَ — root ب و ب. Abwāb is the plural of bāb, a door. Mercy is pictured as a building with many ways in.
وَإِذَا خَرَجَ فَلْيَقُلِ
Wa idhā kharaja fal-yaquli
On the way out, a different duʿāʾ, matched to what you are walking into.
خَرَجَ — root خ ر ج. The going out is treated as its own moment worth marking.
اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ
Allāhumma innī asʾaluka min faḍlik
Leaving for work and provision, you ask for His bounty.
فَضْلِكَ — root ف ض ل. Faḍl is what is given over and above what is owed. Rizq is sought from it.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

Walking In: Ask for the Mercy Doors

As you step into the masjid — right foot first — you say: Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy. Think about what you’re actually doing: you’re walking into Allah’s house, so you ask for the thing that house is full of. Mercy.

It’s a tiny habit that flips your mindset at the door. You’re not just “going to pray” — you’re walking into a space you’re asking Allah to fill with mercy for you.

🌱 A gentle check-upThis week: right foot in, and say the mercy duʿāʾ every single time before anything else.
Entering the Masjid

On entering the masjid with the right foot, one says: “O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy.” It frames the visit as a seeking of Allah’s mercy in His house.

A small, consistent habit that sets the heart’s intention at the threshold.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: how might this duʿāʾ change the way you enter a masjid?
اللَّهُمَّAllāhummaO Allahnounأ-ل-ه
افْتَحْ لِيiftaḥ līopen for meverbف-ت-ح
أَبْوَابَabwābathe gates ofnounب-و-ب
رَحْمَتِكَraḥmatikYour mercynounر-ح-م
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Notice the direction of each duʿāʾ. Walking into the house of Allah, you ask for the doors of His mercy to open. Walking out into the world of work and errands, you ask for a share of His bounty (rizq). Islam frames the masjid as the source and the marketplace as the search.
✅ Quick checkWhat is said on entering the masjid?
اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ“O Allah, open for me the gates of Your mercy.”
Walking Out: Ask for the Bounty

Leaving — left foot first — the duʿāʾ changes: Allah, I ask You of Your bounty. Why the switch from mercy to bounty? Because you’re heading back out into the world of work, study, and errands, where you need Allah’s rizq (provision).

Together, the two du’as map your whole day: you go into the masjid for mercy, and back out for provision — both from Allah, start to finish.

🌱 A gentle check-upLeft foot out, and say the bounty duʿāʾ — then go earn your day knowing where rizq really comes from.
Leaving the Masjid

On leaving the masjid with the left foot, one says: “O Allah, I ask You of Your bounty,” turning outward to seek provision after seeking mercy within.

The paired supplications connect worship and daily livelihood, both sought from Allah.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: do you consciously seek provision from Allah as you return to daily life?

أَسْأَلُكَasʾalukaask Youverbس-أ-ل
مِنْ فَضْلِكَmin faḍlikof Your bountynounف-ض-ل
💡 Right in, left out
A simple, memorable sunnah: enter with the right foot (honour), leave with the left. It is a small habit that keeps the whole visit wrapped in remembrance.
✅ Quick checkWhat is said on leaving?
اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ“O Allah, I ask You of Your bounty.”
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
For one week, don’t cross a masjid threshold in silence. Right foot in with اللَّهُمَّ افْتَحْ لِي أَبْوَابَ رَحْمَتِكَ, left foot out with اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَسْأَلُكَ مِنْ فَضْلِكَ.

Chapter 10 — The Opening Supplication
الدُّعَاءُ — اِحْفَظْ وَاعْمَلْ

Workbook — said silently after the opening takbīr, before al-Fātiḥah.

About this itemمَتَى وَكَيْف · When & how
When
بَعْدَ تَكْبِيرَةِ الإِحْرَامِ — after the opening takbīr, before al-Fātiḥah
How
Said silently to oneself; choose one authentic wording
Purpose
Opening the prayer with praise and a plea for purification
Source
أَهْلُ السُّنَن · the Sunan; and مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْه · Bukhārī & Muslim
١
كَانَ عُمَرُ بْنُ الخَطَّابِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ إِذَا اسْتَفْتَحَ الصَّلَاةَ قَالَWhen ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may Allāh be pleased with him) opened the prayer he would say

Subḥānaka-llāhumma wa-bi-ḥamdik, wa-tabāraka-smuk, wa-taʿālā jadduk, wa-lā ilāha ghayruk

قَالَ أَبُو هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُAbū Hurayrah (may Allāh be pleased with him) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ إِذَا كَبَّرَ فِي الصَّلَاةِ، سَكَتَ هُنَيَّةً قَبْلَ أَنْ يَقْرَأَ. فَقُلْتُ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ بِأَبِي أَنْتَ وَأُمِّي، أَرَأَيْتَ سُكُوتَكَ بَيْنَ التَّكْبِيرِ وَالقِرَاءَةِ، مَا تَقُولُ؟ قَالَ: أَقُولُ: اللَّهُمَّ بَاعِدْ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا بَاعَدْتَ بَيْنَ المَشْرِقِ وَالمَغْرِبِ. اللَّهُمَّ نَقِّنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا يُنَقَّى الثَّوْبُ الأَبْيَضُ مِنَ الدَّنَسِ. اللَّهُمَّ اغْسِلْنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ بِالثَّلْجِ وَالمَاءِ وَالبَرَدِ»

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْSay quietly after the opening takbīr, before the recitation.
اللَّهُمَّ بَاعِدْ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا بَاعَدْتَ بَيْنَ المَشْرِقِ وَالمَغْرِبِ. اللَّهُمَّ نَقِّنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا يُنَقَّى الثَّوْبُ الأَبْيَضُ مِنَ الدَّنَسِ. اللَّهُمَّ اغْسِلْنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ بِالثَّلْجِ وَالمَاءِ وَالبَرَدِ
✎Added by us

“The Prophet ﷺ, when he said the takbīr in the prayer, would fall silent for a moment before reciting. So I said: O Messenger of Allāh, may my father and my mother be given for you, tell me about your silence between the takbīr and the recitation, what do you say? He said: I say: ‘O Allāh, put distance between me and my sins as You have put distance between the east and the west. O Allāh, cleanse me of my sins as a white garment is cleansed of filth. O Allāh, wash me of my sins with snow, water and hail.’”

Kāna-n-nabiyyu ﷺ idhā kabbara fī-ṣ-ṣalāti, sakata hunayyatan qabla an yaqraʾ. Fa-qultu: Yā rasūla-llāhi bi-abī anta wa-ummī, a-raʾayta sukūtaka bayna-t-takbīri wa-l-qirāʾati, mā taqūl? Qāla: Aqūlu: Allāhumma bāʿid baynī wa-bayna khaṭāyāya kamā bāʿadta bayna-l-mashriqi wa-l-maghrib. Allāhumma naqqinī min khaṭāyāya kamā yunaqqā-th-thawbu-l-abyaḍu mina-d-danas. Allāhumma-ghsilnī min khaṭāyāya bi-th-thalji wa-l-māʾi wa-l-barad

Abū Hurayrah noticed the silence and asked what was filling it.
بِأَبِي — root أ ب و. 'By my father and my mother' is a formula of love: I would give them for you.
قَالَ: أَقُولُ: اللَّهُمَّ بَاعِدْ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا بَاعَدْتَ بَيْنَ المَشْرِقِ وَالمَغْرِبِ
Qāla: Aqūlu: Allāhumma bāʿid baynī wa-bayna khaṭāyāya kamā bāʿadta bayna-l-mashriqi wa-l-maghrib
The first request is distance from sin, measured against the widest distance there is.
بَاعِدْ — root ب ع د. Form III, to place far off. He asks for separation, not only for pardon.
اللَّهُمَّ نَقِّنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ كَمَا يُنَقَّى الثَّوْبُ الأَبْيَضُ مِنَ الدَّنَسِ
Allāhumma naqqinī min khaṭāyāya kamā yunaqqā-th-thawbu-l-abyaḍu mina-d-danas
Then cleansing: the mark has to come out, the way it comes out of white cloth.
نَقِّنِي — root ن ق و. The book glosses naqqinī as: purify me. White cloth shows every stain, which is why it is the example given.
اللَّهُمَّ اغْسِلْنِي مِنْ خَطَايَايَ بِالثَّلْجِ وَالمَاءِ وَالبَرَدِ
Allāhumma-ghsilnī min khaṭāyāya bi-th-thalji wa-l-māʾi wa-l-barad
Then washing, named with three cold and clean things.
وَالبَرَدِ — root ب ر د. The book: hail is frozen water that comes down from cloud in small pieces.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
هُنَيَّةًأَيْ: يَسِيراً مِنَ الوَقْتِ
hunayyah — a short whileThat is: a little of time.
نَقِّنِيأَيْ: طَهِّرْنِي
naqqinī — cleanse meThat is: purify me.
الدَّنَسِأَيِ: الوَسَخ
al-danas — filthThat is: dirt.
البَرَدُالبَرَدُ: مَاءٌ مُتَجَمِّدٌ يَنْزِلُ مِنَ السَّحَابِ قِطَعاً صِغَاراً
al-barad — hailAl-barad: frozen water that comes down from the clouds in small pieces.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٣
كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ إِذَا قَامَ إِلَى الصَّلَاةِ قَالَWhen the Prophet ﷺ stood for prayer he would say
الكِتَابFrom the book

«وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِيَ لِلَّذِي فَطَرَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضَ حَنِيفاً، وَمَا أَنَا مِنَ المُشْرِكِينَ. إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي وَمَحْيَايَ وَمَمَاتِي لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العَالَمِينَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، وَبِذَلِكَ أُمِرْتُ، وَأَنَا مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ. اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ المَلِكُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ. أَنْتَ رَبِّي، وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ. ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي، وَاعْتَرَفْتُ بِذَنْبِي. فَاغْفِرْ لِي ذُنُوبِي جَمِيعاً؛ إِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ. وَاهْدِنِي لِأَحْسَنِ الأَخْلَاقِ؛ لَا يَهْدِي لِأَحْسَنِهَا إِلَّا أَنْتَ. وَاصْرِفْ عَنِّي سَيِّئَهَا؛ لَا يَصْرِفُ عَنِّي سَيِّئَهَا إِلَّا أَنْتَ. لَبَّيْكَ وَسَعْدَيْكَ، وَالخَيْرُ كُلُّهُ فِي يَدَيْكَ، وَالشَّرُّ لَيْسَ إِلَيْكَ. أَنَا بِكَ وَإِلَيْكَ، تَبَارَكْتَ وَتَعَالَيْتَ. أَسْتَغْفِرُكَ وَأَتُوبُ إِلَيْكَ»

✎Added by us

“I have turned my face to the One who originated the heavens and the earth, inclining to Him alone, and I am not one of those who associate others with Him. My prayer, my sacrifice, my living and my dying belong to Allāh, Lord of the worlds. He has no partner. With this I was commanded, and I am one of the Muslims. O Allāh, You are the King; there is no god but You. You are my Lord and I am Your servant. I have wronged myself and I admit my sin, so forgive me all my sins; none forgives sins but You. Guide me to the best of characters; none guides to the best of them but You. Turn away from me its worst; none turns its worst away from me but You. Here I am at Your call, glad to answer You. All good is in Your hands, and evil is not ascribed to You. I am by You and to You I turn. Blessed are You and exalted are You. I seek Your forgiveness and I repent to You.”

Wajjahtu wajhiya lilladhī faṭara-s-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa ḥanīfan, wa-mā anā mina-l-mushrikīn. Inna ṣalātī wa-nusukī wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātī li-llāhi rabbi-l-ʿālamīn, lā sharīka lah, wa-bi-dhālika umirt, wa-anā mina-l-muslimīn. Allāhumma anta-l-maliku lā ilāha illā ant. Anta rabbī, wa-anā ʿabduk. Ẓalamtu nafsī, wa-ʿtaraftu bi-dhanbī. Fa-ghfir lī dhunūbī jamīʿan; innahu lā yaghfiru-dh-dhunūba illā ant. Wa-hdinī li-aḥsani-l-akhlāq; lā yahdī li-aḥsanihā illā ant. Wa-ṣrif ʿannī sayyiʾahā; lā yaṣrifu ʿannī sayyiʾahā illā ant. Labbayka wa-saʿdayk, wa-l-khayru kulluhu fī yadayk, wa-sh-sharru laysa ilayk. Anā bika wa-ilayk, tabārakta wa-taʿālayt. Astaghfiruka wa-atūbu ilayk

Wajjahtu wajhiya lilladhī faṭara-s-samāwāti wa-l-arḍa ḥanīfan, wa-mā anā mina-l-mushrikīn
Turning the face means directing worship to the Creator and to no one beside Him.
وَجَّهْتُ — root و ج ه. The book glosses 'wajjahtu wajhiya' as: I made my worship purely for Him. Ḥanīf, it adds, is one who leans away from shirk toward tawḥīd.
إِنَّ صَلَاتِي وَنُسُكِي وَمَحْيَايَ وَمَمَاتِي لِلَّهِ رَبِّ العَالَمِينَ، لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، وَبِذَلِكَ أُمِرْتُ، وَأَنَا مِنَ المُسْلِمِينَ
Inna ṣalātī wa-nusukī wa-maḥyāya wa-mamātī li-llāhi rabbi-l-ʿālamīn, lā sharīka lah, wa-bi-dhālika umirt, wa-anā mina-l-muslimīn
Prayer, sacrifice, life and death are all handed over to one Owner.
وَنُسُكِي — root ن س ك. The book glosses nusukī plainly: my slaughtering. Worship with the body and worship with wealth, both named.
اللَّهُمَّ أَنْتَ المَلِكُ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ. أَنْتَ رَبِّي، وَأَنَا عَبْدُكَ. ظَلَمْتُ نَفْسِي، وَاعْتَرَفْتُ بِذَنْبِي. فَاغْفِرْ لِي ذُنُوبِي جَمِيعاً
Allāhumma anta-l-maliku lā ilāha illā ant. Anta rabbī, wa-anā ʿabduk. Ẓalamtu nafsī, wa-ʿtaraftu bi-dhanbī. Fa-ghfir lī dhunūbī jamīʿan
He names Allāh as King, admits his own wrong, and only then asks.
وَاعْتَرَفْتُ — root ع ر ف. Iʿtirāf is saying out loud what you already know. The request comes after the admission, not before it.
إِنَّهُ لَا يَغْفِرُ الذُّنُوبَ إِلَّا أَنْتَ. وَاهْدِنِي لِأَحْسَنِ الأَخْلَاقِ؛ لَا يَهْدِي لِأَحْسَنِهَا إِلَّا أَنْتَ
innahu lā yaghfiru-dh-dhunūba illā ant. Wa-hdinī li-aḥsani-l-akhlāq; lā yahdī li-aḥsanihā illā ant
Forgiveness and guidance are both traced back to one source.
لِأَحْسَنِ — root ح س ن. Not simply good character but the best of it. The superlative is chosen on purpose.
وَاصْرِفْ عَنِّي سَيِّئَهَا؛ لَا يَصْرِفُ عَنِّي سَيِّئَهَا إِلَّا أَنْتَ. لَبَّيْكَ وَسَعْدَيْكَ
Wa-ṣrif ʿannī sayyiʾahā; lā yaṣrifu ʿannī sayyiʾahā illā ant. Labbayka wa-saʿdayk
He asks also to be steered away from bad character, then answers Allāh's call.
وَسَعْدَيْكَ — root س ع د. The book glosses it: I have answered You, my Lord, to what You called me to, and I am glad of it.
وَالخَيْرُ كُلُّهُ فِي يَدَيْكَ، وَالشَّرُّ لَيْسَ إِلَيْكَ. أَنَا بِكَ وَإِلَيْكَ، تَبَارَكْتَ وَتَعَالَيْتَ. أَسْتَغْفِرُكَ وَأَتُوبُ إِلَيْكَ
wa-l-khayru kulluhu fī yadayk, wa-sh-sharru laysa ilayk. Anā bika wa-ilayk, tabārakta wa-taʿālayt. Astaghfiruka wa-atūbu ilayk
Good is in His hands, evil is not ascribed to Him, and the duʿāʾ ends in repentance.
تَبَارَكْتَ — root ب ر ك. The book: You have reached the utmost in blessing. And taʿālayta: You have reached the utmost in highness.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
وَجَّهْتُ وَجْهِيَأَيْ: أَخْلَصْتُ عِبَادَتِي
wajjahtu wajhiya — I have turned my faceThat is: I have made my worship sincerely for Him.
فَطَرَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضَأَيْ: خَلَقَهُمَا وَأَبْدَعَهُمَا عَلَى غَيْرِ مِثَالٍ سَبَقَ
faṭara al-samāwāti wa-l-arḍ — He originated the heavens and the earthThat is: He created them and brought them into being with no prior model.
حَنِيفاًأَيْ: مَائِلاً عَنِ الشِّرْكِ إِلَى التَّوْحِيدِ
ḥanīfan — inclining to pure monotheismThat is: turning away from polytheism toward the oneness of Allāh.
وَنُسُكِيأَيْ: ذَبْحِي
wa-nusukī — and my sacrificeThat is: my slaughtering.
وَسَعْدَيْكَأَيْ: أَجَبْتُكَ يَا رَبِّ إِلَى مَا دَعَوْتَنِي إِلَيْهِ، وَأَنَا سَعِيدٌ بِذَلِكَ
wa-saʿdayka — and at Your serviceThat is: I have answered You, my Lord, to what You called me to, and I am glad of that.
وَإِلَيْكَأَيْ: أَنَا أَسْتَعِينُ بِكَ وَأَتَوَجَّهُ إِلَيْكَ
wa-ilayka — and unto YouThat is: I seek help from You and I turn toward You.
تَبَارَكْتَأَيْ: بَلَغْتَ فِي البَرَكَةِ الغَايَةَ
tabārakta — You are blessedThat is: You have reached the utmost in blessing.
وَتَعَالَيْتَأَيْ: بَلَغْتَ مِنَ العُلُوِّ الغَايَةَ
wa-taʿālayta — and You are exaltedThat is: You have reached the utmost in loftiness.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

٤
كَانَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ إِذَا قَامَ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ افْتَتَحَ صَلَاتَهُWhen the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ rose at night he would open his prayer
الكِتَابFrom the book

«اللَّهُمَّ رَبَّ جَبْرَائِيلَ، وَمِيكَائِيلَ، وَإِسْرَافِيلَ، فَاطِرَ السَّمَوَاتِ وَالأَرْضِ، عَالِمَ الغَيْبِ وَالشَّهَادَةِ، أَنْتَ تَحْكُمُ بَيْنَ عِبَادِكَ فِيمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَخْتَلِفُونَ. اهْدِنِي لِمَا اخْتُلِفَ فِيهِ مِنَ الحَقِّ بِإِذْنِكَ؛ إِنَّكَ تَهْدِي مَنْ تَشَاءُ إِلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ»

✎Added by us

“O Allāh, Lord of Jibrāʾīl, Mīkāʾīl and Isrāfīl, Originator of the heavens and the earth, Knower of the unseen and the seen, You judge between Your servants concerning what they used to differ over. Guide me to the truth in what has been disputed, by Your permission. You guide whom You will to a straight path.”

Allāhumma rabba Jabrāʾīla, wa-Mīkāʾīla, wa-Isrāfīla, fāṭira-s-samāwāti wa-l-arḍi, ʿālima-l-ghaybi wa-sh-shahādati, anta taḥkumu bayna ʿibādika fīmā kānū fīhi yakhtalifūn. Ihdinī limā-khtulifa fīhi mina-l-ḥaqqi bi-idhnik; innaka tahdī man tashāʾu ilā ṣirāṭin mustaqīm

He opens by naming the Lord of the three greatest angels.
رَبَّ — root ر ب ب. Even these angels are addressed as belonging to Him, not as powers of their own.

Two descriptions: He brought creation into being, and nothing is hidden from Him.
فَاطِرَ — root ف ط ر. The book glosses faṭara as: He created and originated them on no pattern that came before.
أَنْتَ تَحْكُمُ بَيْنَ عِبَادِكَ فِيمَا كَانُوا فِيهِ يَخْتَلِفُونَ

Disputes people cannot settle here will be settled by Him.

اهْدِنِي لِمَا اخْتُلِفَ فِيهِ مِنَ الحَقِّ بِإِذْنِكَ؛ إِنَّكَ تَهْدِي مَنْ تَشَاءُ إِلَى صِرَاطٍ مُسْتَقِيمٍ

The request is to be shown which side of a disputed matter is the truth.
بِإِذْنِكَ — root أ ذ ن. Guidance is asked for as permission granted, not as something earned.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

Warming Up With Pure Praise

Before you recite a single verse, you open the prayer with straight-up praise: Glory be to You, O Allah — blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, there’s no god but You. It’s like tuning your heart before the main event. You’re reminding yourself exactly Who you’re standing in front of.

Say it slowly. Every phrase is you telling Allah: You are far above any flaw, Your name alone is blessed, and nobody compares to You. That mindset carries into the rest of the prayer.

🌱 A gentle check-upPick subḥānak… and use it in every prayer this week. Say it slow enough to actually mean it.
Opening With Glorification

After the opening takbīr, one says silently: “Glory be to You, O Allah, and all praise; blessed is Your name, exalted is Your majesty, and there is no god but You.” It begins the prayer with pure praise of Allah.

Beginning with glorification orients the heart before recitation.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: how does opening with praise shape the prayer that follows?

💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Before you even recite al-Fātiḥah, you open with pure praise of Allah — subḥānak (You are far above any flaw), tabāraka-smuk (Your very name is blessed). It sets the heart in the right posture for everything that follows: you are standing before the Perfect One.
💡 Pick one, learn it well
Both openings are authentic. Choose one to memorise first — subḥānak… is the shortest — and you can rotate the other in later. Either is said silently, only to yourself.
✅ Quick checkWhat is the shortest authentic opening supplication?
سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ…“Subḥānaka-llāhumma wa bi-ḥamdik…”
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
The second wording is a plea for a clean slate, painted in three vivid images — distance from sin like east from west, a white garment scrubbed clean, a washing with water, snow, and hail. You begin the prayer asking to be made spotless for the meeting with your Lord.
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
Memorise سُبْحَانَكَ اللَّهُمَّ وَبِحَمْدِكَ… and use it in every prayer this week. Say it slowly enough to mean each phrase before you begin al-Fātiḥah.

A Companion says plainly that he cannot hold his attention in prayer.
يَلْبِسُهَا — root ل ب س. The book explains: he placed a barrier of whispering between me and a complete prayer, blocking khushūʿ.
فَقَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ: ذَاكَ شَيْطَانٌ يُقَالُ لَهُ: خِنْزَبٌ
Fa-qāla-n-nabiyyu ﷺ: Dhāka shayṭānun yuqālu lahu: Khinzab
The trouble is named, and naming it cuts it down to size.
خِنْزَبٌ — Khinzab is a proper name for the devil who works at disturbing prayer. The answer given is not 'try harder' but knowing who is doing this.
فَإِذَا أَحْسَسْتَهُ؛ فَتَعَوَّذْ بِاللَّهِ مِنْهُ، وَاتْفِلْ عَلَى يَسَارِكَ - ثَلَاثاً

Two things to do the moment you notice him: take refuge, and spit lightly leftward three times.
وَاتْفِلْ — root ت ف ل. The book: tafl is a puff of air carrying a little saliva. Not a full spit.
قَالَ: فَفَعَلْتُ ذَلِكَ؛ فَأَذْهَبَهُ اللَّهُ عَنِّي

He acted on the instruction and the trouble left him.
فَأَذْهَبَهُ — root ذ ه ب. Form IV: Allāh made him go. The man acted; the removal was Allāh's doing.

رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُدَReported by Abū Dāwūd

Body Low, Lord High

Rukūʿ is the first big bow of the prayer, and the words match the motion perfectly: Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great. Your back goes down; your words lift Allah up. You’re making a physical statement — only He is truly great, and I’m His servant.

The minimum is three times, but that’s a floor, not a target. The Prophet ﷺ often added “O Allah, forgive me” — turning the bow into both praise and a request.

🌱 A gentle check-upIn every rukūʿ this week, say the tasbīḥ three full times — no rushing the bow.
Glorifying Allah in Rukūʿ

In the bowing, one says “Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great” at least three times. The Prophet ﷺ would also add “Glory be to You, O Allah… O Allah, forgive me.”

The lowered posture is paired with words declaring Allah’s greatness.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: does your rukūʿ give you time to mean the words three times over?
سُبْحَانَsubḥānaglory be tonounس-ب-ح
رَبِّيَrabbiyamy Lordnounر-ب-ب
العَظِيمِal-ʿaẓīmthe Most Greatnounع-ظ-م
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
The posture and the words match: as the body bows low, the tongue proclaims Allah’s greatness — al-ʿAẓīm, the Most Great. Rukūʿ is a physical statement that only He is truly great, and you are His servant.
✅ Quick checkWhat is the tasbīḥ of rukūʿ?
سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ العَظِيمِ“Glory be to my Lord, the Most Great.”
⭐ Say it three, mean it more
The minimum is three times, but the number is a floor, not a ceiling. ʿĀʾishah (رضي الله عنها) reported the Prophet ﷺ would often add subḥānaka-llāhumma… Allāhumma-ghfir lī — pairing glorification with a plea for forgiveness.
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
In every rukūʿ this week, slow down enough to say سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ العَظِيمِ three full times — no rushing. Feel the meaning: He is great, and you are low before Him.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

He Hears — So Say It Like You Mean It

As you come up from the bow you say samiʿa-llāhu liman ḥamidah — “Allah hears whoever praises Him.” But “hears” here means hears and responds. You’re announcing that praising Allah is never wasted breath: He’s listening, and He answers.

Then standing straight, you pour on the praise: “our Lord, to You is all praise — abundant, good, and blessed.” There’s a hadith of angels racing to write down whoever says this well, so it’s worth a moment of real focus.

🌱 A gentle check-upStand fully upright before you say the ḥamd — then say it with actual gratitude, not on autopilot.
Praise on Rising

On rising from rukūʿ the imam and one praying alone say “Allah hears whoever praises Him,” and standing upright everyone says “our Lord, to You is all praise,” optionally with the fuller wording.

The phrase affirms that Allah both hears and answers the one who praises Him.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: do you pause to stand fully and praise, or rush through the standing?
سَمِعَ اللَّهُsamiʿa-llāhAllah hears/answersverbس-م-ع
لِمَنْlimanwhoeverparticle
حَمِدَهُḥamidahpraised Himverbح-م-د
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Samiʿa-llāhu liman ḥamidah doesn’t just mean “Allah hears” — it means He hears in order to respond. You rise announcing that praising Allah is never in vain: He listens and He answers.

⭐ A race to say the ḥamd
The Prophet ﷺ told of angels rushing to record the one who says the fuller rabbanā wa laka-l-ḥamd… with sincerity — so these are words worth saying with presence, not on autopilot.
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
As you rise from rukūʿ, don’t mumble the ḥamd on the way up. Stand fully, then say رَبَّنَا وَلَكَ الحَمْدُ حَمْدًا كَثِيرًا طَيِّبًا مُبَارَكًا فِيهِ with real gratitude.

wa-awwalahu wa-ākhirah, wa-ʿalāniyatahu wa-sirrah
Time and visibility are both covered: early and late, seen and unseen.
وَعَلَانِيَتَهُ — root ع ل ن. ʿAlāniyah is what is done in the open. It is paired with sirr, what is kept private.

دِقَّهُ وَجِلَّهُأَيْ: صَغِيرَهُ وَكَبِيرَهُ

كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ إِذَا سَجَدَ قَالَWhen the Prophet ﷺ prostrated he would say
الكِتَابFrom the book

«اللَّهُمَّ لَكَ سَجَدْتُ، وَبِكَ آمَنْتُ، وَلَكَ أَسْلَمْتُ. سَجَدَ وَجْهِي لِلَّذِي خَلَقَهُ وَصَوَّرَهُ، وَشَقَّ سَمْعَهُ وَبَصَرَهُ. تَبَارَكَ اللَّهُ أَحْسَنُ الخَالِقِينَ»

✎Added by us

“O Allāh, to You I have prostrated, in You I have believed, and to You I have submitted. My face has prostrated to the One who created it and shaped it, and opened its hearing and its sight. Blessed is Allāh, the best of creators.”

Allāhumma laka sajadtu, wa-bika āmantu, wa-laka aslamt. Sajada wajhī lilladhī khalaqahu wa-ṣawwarah, wa-shaqqa samʿahu wa-baṣarah. Tabāraka-llāhu aḥsanu-l-khāliqīn

The prostration, the belief and the submission are all directed to Allāh.
سَجَدْتُ — root س ج د. Sujūd is putting the highest part of you on the ground. Note that 'laka', for You, comes before the verb.
سَجَدَ وَجْهِي لِلَّذِي خَلَقَهُ وَصَوَّرَهُ، وَشَقَّ سَمْعَهُ وَبَصَرَهُ

The face on the ground belongs to the One who made that face work at all.
وَشَقَّ — root ش ق ق. The book glosses shaqqa as: He opened. Hearing and sight were cut open in a face that had neither.

It closes with praise of the Maker rather than with a request.
أَحْسَنُ — root ح س ن. Aḥsan al-khāliqīn: the best of those who shape and form, since bringing into being is His alone.

wa-shaqqa — and He splitThat is: He opened.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

The Lowest You Go, the Highest He Is

Sujūd is the lowest your body gets — forehead on the ground — and the words go the opposite direction: Glory be to my Lord, the Most High. Compare it to rukūʿ, where you said “the Most Great.” The deeper you drop, the higher you declare Him. It’s a beautiful mirror.

And here’s the secret weapon: the Prophet ﷺ said you’re never closer to Allah than in sujūd, so “make lots of duʿāʾ.” After the tasbīḥ, this is the prime spot to ask Him for literally anything.

🌱 A gentle check-upAfter the three tasbīḥs, add one real duʿāʾ of your own in sujūd — you’re as close as it gets.
Glorifying Allah in Sujūd

In prostration one says “Glory be to my Lord, the Most High” at least three times. The Prophet ﷺ taught that the servant is nearest to his Lord in prostration, so one should make much supplication there.

The lowest posture is paired with declaring Allah the Most High, and is the closest moment to Him.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: are you using sujūd — the closest moment — to ask Allah for what you need?
سُبْحَانَsubḥānaglory be tonounس-ب-ح
رَبِّيَrabbiyamy Lordnounر-ب-ب
الأَعْلَىal-aʿlāthe Most Highnounع-ل-و
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
In rukūʿ you said al-ʿAẓīm (the Most Great); in sujūd, the lowest posture, you say al-Aʿlā (the Most High). The lower your body goes, the higher you declare your Lord to be — the two are perfectly matched.
✅ Quick checkWhat is the tasbīḥ of sujūd?
سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ الأَعْلَى“Glory be to my Lord, the Most High.”
⭐ Closest to Him in sujūd
The Prophet ﷺ said the servant is nearest to his Lord while prostrating, so “make much duʿāʾ.” After the tasbīḥ, this is the best moment in the prayer to ask Allah for anything you need.
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
After saying سُبْحَانَ رَبِّيَ الأَعْلَى three times, add one heartfelt duʿāʾ of your own in the next sujūd — you are as close to Allah as you will be in the whole prayer.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«قُولُوا: التَّحِيَّاتُ لِلَّهِ، وَالصَّلَوَاتُ، وَالطَّيِّبَاتُ. السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ. السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ. أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّداً عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ»

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْSay sitting in the tashahhud.
التَّحِيَّاتُ لِلَّهِ، وَالصَّلَوَاتُ، وَالطَّيِّبَاتُ. السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ. السَّلَامُ عَلَيْنَا وَعَلَى عِبَادِ اللَّهِ الصَّالِحِينَ. أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّداً عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
✎Added by us

“Say: All words of honour belong to Allāh, and all prayers, and all good deeds. Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allāh and His blessings. Peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allāh. I bear witness that there is no god but Allāh, and I bear witness that Muḥammad is His servant and His Messenger.”

Qūlū: At-taḥiyyātu li-llāh, wa-ṣ-ṣalawātu, wa-ṭ-ṭayyibāt. As-salāmu ʿalayka ayyuhā-n-nabiyyu wa-raḥmatu-llāhi wa-barakātuh. As-salāmu ʿalaynā wa-ʿalā ʿibādi-llāhi-ṣ-ṣāliḥīn. Ash-hadu an lā ilāha illa-llāh, wa-ash-hadu anna Muḥammadan ʿabduhu wa-rasūluh

Qūlū: At-taḥiyyātu li-llāh, wa-ṣ-ṣalawātu, wa-ṭ-ṭayyibāt
Three kinds of worship are handed over to Allāh at the start of the sitting.
التَّحِيَّاتُ — The book: all expressions of reverence belong to Allāh, by ownership and by right. It glosses ṣalawāt as all supplications, ṭayyibāt as all good deeds.
السَّلَامُ عَلَيْكَ أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ وَرَحْمَةُ اللَّهِ وَبَرَكَاتُهُ

Peace is offered to the Prophet ﷺ, with mercy and blessing named alongside it.

Then peace for yourself and for every righteous servant of Allāh.
الصَّالِحِينَ — root ص ل ح. A ṣāliḥ is one whose state is sound. Praying for them puts you among them.
أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَأَشْهَدُ أَنَّ مُحَمَّداً عَبْدُهُ وَرَسُولُهُ
Ash-hadu an lā ilāha illa-llāh, wa-ash-hadu anna Muḥammadan ʿabduhu wa-rasūluh
The sitting ends with the two testimonies, given as witness rather than opinion.
عَبْدُهُ — root ع ب د. Servant is mentioned before Messenger. His honour starts with belonging to Allāh.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

The Whole of Faith, Sitting Down

The tashahhud packs an entire worldview into a few lines. First it hands all honour and worship to Allah alone. Then it sends peace — on the Prophet ﷺ, on yourself, and on every righteous servant of Allah anywhere. Then it re-states the shahādah, the two testimonies your whole religion stands on.

It’s not a formality to rush before you finish. It’s you renewing everything you believe, every single prayer, sitting quietly before your Lord.

🌱 A gentle check-upLearn it one line at a time — greetings, then peace, then the testimonies — until the whole thing flows.
The Tashahhud

Sitting in prayer, one recites the tashahhud: directing all greetings and worship to Allah, sending peace upon the Prophet ﷺ, upon oneself, and upon the righteous, and affirming the two testimonies of faith.

It is a concise renewal of belief within every prayer, and a pillar of the final sitting.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: do you recite the tashahhud with attention, or rush it before the salām?

💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
The tashahhud is a tiny masterclass in worship: it hands all forms of honour and worship to Allah alone (at-taḥiyyātu lillāh), sends peace, and closes by re-affirming the two testimonies of faith. You renew your whole ʿaqīdah in a single sitting.
⭐ Peace on the righteous, and on you
When you say “peace be upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah,” that salām reaches every righteous servant in the heavens and the earth — and, the Prophet ﷺ noted, it returns to include you.
✅ Quick checkTo whom belong “all greetings, prayers, and good things”?
لِلَّهِTo Allah.
Sending Ṣalāh on the One You Love

After honouring Allah, you turn to the Prophet ﷺ and ask Allah to praise and bless him — tying his family to the family of Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام), the way believers have prayed for centuries. It’s the complete, beloved wording the Prophet ﷺ taught us himself.

Think of it as giving back: he ﷺ carried this message to you across 1,400 years, and here you are asking Allah to raise him higher. It’s a right he has over every believer, and you get to fulfil it several times a day.

🌱 A gentle check-upOnce the tashahhud is solid, add the ṣalāh Ibrāhīmiyyah the same way — a line or two at a time.
Ṣalāh Upon the Prophet ﷺ

After the tashahhud, one sends ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ, asking Allah to praise and bless him and his family as He did Ibrāhīm and his family.

This is the complete taught wording and fulfils a right the Prophet ﷺ has over the believers.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: do you send ṣalāh on the Prophet ﷺ with awareness of what he conveyed to you?
💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
After honouring Allah, you send ṣalāh on His Messenger ﷺ, tying his household to the household of Ibrāhīm (عليه السلام). It is the beloved, complete way to ask Allah to raise and bless the Prophet ﷺ — a right he has over every believer.
💡 Learn the tashahhud first
The tashahhud is a pillar of the final sitting — the prayer isn’t complete without it — so prioritise memorising it, then add the ṣalāh Ibrāhīmiyyah.
✅ Quick checkWhat is sent after the tashahhud?
الصَّلَاةُ عَلَى النَّبِيِّ ﷺThe ṣalāh upon the Prophet ﷺ.
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
Break the tashahhud into three lines — the greetings, the salām, the two testimonies — and master one line a day. Once it flows, add the ṣalāh الإِبْرَاهِيمِيَّة the same way.

Idhā tashahhada aḥadukum; fal-yastaʿidh bi-llāhi min arbaʿ, yaqūlu
A clear instruction: after the tashahhud, seek refuge from four named things.
فَلْيَسْتَعِذْ — root ع و ذ. Form X, to seek shelter with someone. The lām turns it into a command: let him do it.
اللَّهُمَّ إِنِّي أَعُوذُ بِكَ مِنْ عَذَابِ جَهَنَّمَ. وَمِنْ عَذَابِ القَبْرِ
Allāhumma innī aʿūdhu bika min ʿadhābi jahannam. Wa-min ʿadhābi-l-qabr
The first two are punishments: one in Hell, one in the grave.
عَذَابِ — root ع ذ ب. Both are ʿadhāb. One comes soon after death, the other much later. Neither is passed over.
وَمِنْ فِتْنَةِ المَحْيَا وَالمَمَاتِ
Wa-min fitnati-l-maḥyā wa-l-mamāt
The third is trial in life and trial at the end of it.
المَحْيَا — root ح ي ي. The book glosses this pair: every trial in life and after death.
وَمِنْ شَرِّ فِتْنَةِ المَسِيحِ الدَّجَّالِ
Wa-min sharri fitnati-l-masīḥi-d-dajjāl
The fourth is named on its own, the greatest trial before the Hour.
الدَّجَّالِ — root د ج ل. A dajjāl is one who covers truth over with lies. He is also called al-Masīḥ, which is why al-Dajjāl is added.

The first refuge sought is from cowardice, a fault of the heart.

فِتْنَةِ — root ف ت ن. Fitnah is testing metal in fire to see what it really is. Ease tests as surely as loss does.

Wa-aʿūdhu bika min ʿadhābi-l-qabr
Last, the punishment of the grave, the one nobody watching can see.
القَبْرِ — root ق ب ر. The grave is spoken of as either punishment or rest, so refuge is sought from the first of the two.

Two names of Allāh, then the testimony that closes the prayer.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

Shields Up Before You Leave

Right before you say salām and end the prayer, the Prophet ﷺ told us to take cover from the four biggest dangers: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trials of living and dying, and the fitnah of the Dajjāl. He didn’t suggest it — he commanded it.

Think of it like putting your shields up before stepping out. You’ve just spent the prayer close to Allah; the last thing you do is ask Him to protect you from the things that could ruin you forever.

🌱 A gentle check-upMemorise the four-refuge duʿāʾ this week and say it in every prayer before the salām.
Seeking Refuge Before Salām

The Prophet ﷺ commanded seeking refuge, before the salām, from four things: the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trial of life and death, and the trial of the Dajjāl.

The prayer closes with a deliberate, taught seeking of Allah’s protection.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: will you make this commanded duʿāʾ a fixed part of every prayer?

💎 الفَائِدَة · Deeper lesson
Before you leave the prayer, you take shelter from the four greatest dangers — the punishment of Hell, the punishment of the grave, the trial of living and dying, and the fitnah of the Dajjāl. The Prophet ﷺ commanded this duʿāʾ, so it is not optional decoration — it is a taught, deliberate seeking of refuge.
💡 Then ask for yourself
This spot — after the tashahhud, before the salām — is one of the best moments to make personal duʿāʾ. The Prophet ﷺ told a Companion to choose “the duʿāʾ he loves most” here. So after the fixed words, ask Allah for whatever is in your heart.
✅ Quick checkHow many things are sought refuge from before the salām?
أَرْبَعَةٌFour.
Ask for Help to Even Worship Him

This one is humbling. The Prophet ﷺ told Muʿādh never to skip it after any prayer: O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well. Notice what you’re asking — not for money or ease, but for help to do the worship itself.

It quietly admits something true: even the good you manage to do is only by Allah’s help. So you finish the prayer asking Him to enable the next one, and the dhikr and gratitude in between.

🌱 A gentle check-upAdd this duʿāʾ after every prayer this week — then make one personal duʿāʾ of your own.
A Plea for Help to Worship

The Prophet ﷺ instructed Muʿādh to say after every prayer: “O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well” — asking Allah to enable the very worship one seeks to offer.

It acknowledges that all good is accomplished only with Allah’s help.

🌱 A gentle check-upReflect: do you ask Allah’s help for the worship itself, not only for worldly needs?
⭐ Never leave it after every prayer
The Prophet ﷺ told Muʿādh (رضي الله عنه) never to leave saying, after every prayer, Allāhumma aʿinnī ʿalā dhikrik wa shukrik wa ḥusni ʿibādatik — a plea that Allah Himself enable the very worship you’re trying to give Him.
✅ Quick checkWhat did the Prophet ﷺ tell Muʿādh to say after every prayer?
اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِكَ وَشُكْرِكَ وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِكَ“O Allah, help me to remember You, thank You, and worship You well.”
✍️ Activityنَشَاط
Memorise the four-refuge duʿāʾ this week and say it in every prayer before the salām. Then add اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِكَ وَشُكْرِكَ وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِكَ — and one duʿāʾ of your own.

When

The prayer is over, and the first thing he does is ask pardon, three times.

You are the One free of every flaw, and safety itself comes only from You.
السَّلَامُ — root س ل م. The book glosses as-Salām as the One free of all defects and deficiencies, and adds that safety from harm and evil is hoped for from Him alone.

tabārakta yā dhā-l-jalāli wa-l-ikrām
Blessing belongs to Him, addressed by two names: overwhelming greatness, and generosity towards His servants.
الجَلَالِ — root ج ل ل. The book glosses al-Jalāl as the One of immense rank. Ikrām is the other side of it: He is honoured, and He honours.

One God, and nothing set alongside Him: the sentence is denial first, then affirmation.
وَحْدَهُ — root و ح د. Waḥdahu is a ḥāl, 'being alone'. It closes the door that lā sharīka lah then bolts.
لَهُ المُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ.
lahu-l-mulku wa-lahu-l-ḥamd, wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr
Ownership, praise and power are all placed with Him and nowhere else.
المُلْكُ — root م ل ك. Al-mulk is not property but sovereignty: the right to decide, not merely to hold.
اللَّهُمَّ لَا مَانِعَ لِمَا أَعْطَيْتَ، وَلَا مُعْطِيَ لِمَا مَنَعْتَ.
Allāhumma lā māniʿa limā aʿṭayt, wa-lā muʿṭiya limā manaʿt
Whatever He hands out, no one intercepts; whatever He holds back, no one releases.
مَانِعَ — root م ن ع. Māniʿ and muʿṭī are active participles, so the denial covers any withholder or giver at all, not one particular case.
وَلَا يَنْفَعُ ذَا الجَدِّ مِنْكَ الجَدُّ
Wa-lā yanfaʿu dha-l-jaddi minka-l-jadd
Wealth, rank and luck buy a man nothing once Allāh has decided.
الجَدُّ — root ج د د. Al-jadd here means fortune, riches, standing. The wording repeats it: the man of fortune is not helped by his fortune.

كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ يَقُولُ فِي دُبُرِ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ حِينَ يُسَلِّمُThe Prophet ﷺ would say at the end of every prayer, when he gave the salām
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ المُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ. لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ. لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَلَا نَعْبُدُ إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ. لَهُ النِّعْمَةُ، وَلَهُ الفَضْلُ، وَلَهُ الثَّنَاءُ الحَسَنُ. لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ، وَلَوْ كَرِهَ الكَافِرُونَ»

↪ Say at the end of every prayer, straight after the salām.

✎Added by us

“There is no god but Allāh, alone, with no partner. His is the dominion and His is the praise, and He is able to do all things. There is no capacity and no strength except by Allāh. There is no god but Allāh, and we worship none but Him. His is the favour, His is the bounty, and His is the beautiful praise. There is no god but Allāh; we keep the religion purely for Him, however much the disbelievers hate it.”

Lā ilāha illa-llāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lah, lahu-l-mulku wa-lahu-l-ḥamd, wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr. Lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh. Lā ilāha illa-llāh, wa-lā naʿbudu illā iyyāh. Lahu-n-niʿmatu, wa-lahu-l-faḍlu, wa-lahu-th-thanāʾu-l-ḥasan. Lā ilāha illa-llāh, mukhliṣīna lahu-d-dīn, wa-law kariha-l-kāfirūn

Lā ilāha illa-llāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lah
The core sentence, with two clauses that shut out any partner.
إِلَّا — root none (particle). Illā after a full negation is what makes the phrase an exception clause, not a mere claim.
لَهُ المُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ.
lahu-l-mulku wa-lahu-l-ḥamd, wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr
Kingship, praise and power are His by right.
قَدِيرٌ — root ق د ر. Qadīr on the intensive faʿīl pattern: power that is complete, not power that is sufficient.
لَا حَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ.
Lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh
We have no room to move and no force to move with unless He supplies it.
حَوْلَ — root ح و ل. Ḥawl is the ability to shift a state; quwwah is the strength to carry it out. Both are borrowed.
لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، وَلَا نَعْبُدُ إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ.
Lā ilāha illa-llāh, wa-lā naʿbudu illā iyyāh
The belief is stated, then the practice that must follow it.
إِيَّاهُ — root none (pronoun). Iyyāhu is the detached object pronoun, placed after illā because the negation puts the object first in force.
لَهُ النِّعْمَةُ، وَلَهُ الفَضْلُ، وَلَهُ الثَّنَاءُ الحَسَنُ.
Lahu-n-niʿmatu, wa-lahu-l-faḍlu, wa-lahu-th-thanāʾu-l-ḥasan
Every blessing, every unearned extra, and every fair word of praise trace back to Him.
الفَضْلُ — root ف ض ل. Faḍl is what is given beyond what is owed. Niʿmah is the gift itself; faḍl is its generosity.
لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ، مُخْلِصِينَ لَهُ الدِّينَ، وَلَوْ كَرِهَ الكَافِرُونَ
Lā ilāha illa-llāh, mukhliṣīna lahu-d-dīn, wa-law kariha-l-kāfirūn
We say it meaning it, and we do not soften it for anyone who dislikes hearing it.
مُخْلِصِينَ — root خ ل ص. Ikhlāṣ is filtering out everything mixed in. The plural ḥāl mukhliṣīna describes the speakers as they say the words.

A named instruction, and a strong prohibition against dropping it.

fī duburi kulli ṣalātin taqūl

دُبُرِ — root د ب ر. The book glosses dubur as ʿaqib, the heel of a thing: immediately after it ends.
اللَّهُمَّ أَعِنِّي عَلَى ذِكْرِكَ، وَشُكْرِكَ، وَحُسْنِ عِبَادَتِكَ
Allāhumma aʿinnī ʿalā dhikrik, wa-shukrik, wa-ḥusni ʿibādatik
Even remembering and thanking Him needs His help, and so does doing them well.
وَحُسْنِ — root ح س ن. Ḥusn is added to ʿibādah alone: the first two are asked for, the third is asked for in good quality.

رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُدَReported by Abū Dāwūd

٥
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَنْ سَبَّحَ اللَّهَ فِي دُبُرِ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ. وَحَمِدَ اللَّهَ ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ. وَكَبَّرَ اللَّهَ ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ. فَتِلْكَ تِسْعَةٌ وَتِسْعُونَ، وَقَالَ تَمَامَ المِئَةِ: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ المُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ. غُفِرَتْ خَطَايَاهُ؛ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ مِثْلَ زَبَدِ البَحْرِ»

ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ (تَسْبِيحاً)، ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ (تَحْمِيداً)، ثَلَاثاً وَثَلَاثِينَ (تَكْبِيراً)، تَمَامَ المِئَةِthirty-three times (tasbīḥ), thirty-three times (taḥmīd), thirty-three times (takbīr), completing the hundred

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْThirty-three Subḥāna-llāh, thirty-three al-Ḥamdu li-llāh, thirty-three Allāhu akbar, then this once to make a hundred.
لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ وَحْدَهُ لَا شَرِيكَ لَهُ، لَهُ المُلْكُ، وَلَهُ الحَمْدُ، وَهُوَ عَلَى كُلِّ شَيْءٍ قَدِيرٌ
✎Added by us

“Whoever glorifies Allāh thirty-three times at the end of every prayer, and praises Allāh thirty-three times, and magnifies Allāh thirty-three times — that is ninety-nine — and then says, to complete the hundred: ‘There is no god but Allāh, alone, with no partner. His is the dominion and His is the praise, and He is able to do all things’ — his sins are forgiven, even if they were like the foam of the sea.”

Man sabbaḥa-llāha fī duburi kulli ṣalātin thalāthan wa-thalāthīn, wa-ḥamida-llāha thalāthan wa-thalāthīn, wa-kabbara-llāha thalāthan wa-thalāthīn, fa-tilka tisʿatun wa-tisʿūn, wa-qāla tamāma-l-miʾah: Lā ilāha illa-llāhu waḥdahu lā sharīka lah, lahu-l-mulku wa-lahu-l-ḥamd, wa-huwa ʿalā kulli shayʾin qadīr. Ghufirat khaṭāyāh; wa-in kānat mithla zabadi-l-baḥr
