قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَوْلَا أَنْ أَشُقَّ عَلَى أُمَّتِي؛ لَأَمَرْتُهُمْ بِالسِّوَاكِ عِنْدَ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ»

✎Added by us

“Were it not that I would burden my nation, I would have commanded them to use the tooth-stick at every prayer.”

EstablishesThe siwāk before every prayer is strongly encouraged, stopping short of obligation only to spare hardship.

Lawlā an ashuqqa ʿalā ummatī; la-amartuhum bi-s-siwāki ʿinda kulli ṣalāh

Care for the community is what held the command back.
أَشُقَّ — root ش ق ق. Shaqq is splitting; the verb here means to lay hardship on someone. The concern was for what people could carry.
لَأَمَرْتُهُمْ بِالسِّوَاكِ عِنْدَ كُلِّ صَلَاةٍ

The wish behind the words shows how much the act is loved.
لَأَمَرْتُهُمْ — root أ م ر. Amr is a binding order. Since the order was withheld, the siwāk stays recommended rather than required.

كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ إِذَا عَطَسَWhen the Prophet ﷺ sneezed

✎Added by us

He would cover his face with his hand or his garment, and lower his voice with it.

EstablishesA sneeze is covered with the hand or a garment, and its sound is kept low.

The face is covered, by hand or by cloth, whichever is nearer.

Chapter 95 — Yawning

Book p.197 · النَّظَافَةُ — Cleanliness · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

✎Added by us

“Yawning is from Shayṭān. So when one of you yawns, let him hold it back as much as he can. For when one of you says ‘haa’, Shayṭān laughs.”

EstablishesA yawn is to be resisted as far as one is able, and its sound not let out.

At-tathāʾubu mina-sh-shayṭān; fa-idhā tathāʾaba aḥadukum fal-yaruddahu mā-staṭāʿ. Fa-inna aḥadakum idhā qāla: hā; ḍaḥika-sh-shayṭān

The yawn is traced back to a source, which is why it is resisted.
التَّثَاؤُبُ — root ث أ ب. Tathāʾub is the yawn itself. Calling it “from Shayṭān” points at the heaviness and slackness behind it.
فَإِذَا تَثَاءَبَ أَحَدُكُمْ فَلْيَرُدَّهُ مَا اسْتَطَاعَ

Push it back, and only as far as you actually can.
فَلْيَرُدَّهُ — root ر د د. Radd is pushing a thing back the way it came. The clause “as much as he can” keeps the demand within reach.

Letting the sound out openly is what gives Shayṭān his satisfaction.
ضَحِكَ — root ض ح ك. Ḍaḥika is to laugh. The book notes that hā is simply the sound of the yawn being written down.

قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا انْتَعَلَ أَحَدُكُمْ؛ فَلْيَبْدَأْ بِالْيَمِينِ. وَإِذَا نَزَعَ؛ فَلْيَبْدَأْ بِالشِّمَالِ»

✎Added by us

“When one of you puts on footwear, let him begin with the right. And when he takes it off, let him begin with the left.”

EstablishesFootwear goes on the right foot first and comes off the left foot first.

Idhā-ntaʿala aḥadukum; fal-yabdaʾ bi-l-yamīn. Wa idhā nazaʿa; fal-yabdaʾ bi-sh-shimāl

إِذَاwhen
انْتَعَلَputs on footwear
أَحَدُكُمْone of you
فَلْيَبْدَأْlet him begin
بِالْيَمِينِwith the right
وَإِذَاand when
نَزَعَhe takes off
فَلْيَبْدَأْlet him begin
بِالشِّمَالِwith the left
إِذَا انْتَعَلَ أَحَدُكُمْ؛ فَلْيَبْدَأْ بِالْيَمِينِ
Idhā-ntaʿala aḥadukum; fal-yabdaʾ bi-l-yamīn
Putting them on starts with the right foot.
انْتَعَلَ — root ن ع ل. The book explains intaʿala as one of you intending to put his sandal on. The rule applies from the moment he begins.
وَإِذَا نَزَعَ؛ فَلْيَبْدَأْ بِالشِّمَالِ
Wa idhā nazaʿa; fal-yabdaʾ bi-sh-shimāl
Taking them off starts with the left foot.
بِالشِّمَالِ — root ش م ل. Shimāl is the left. Reversing the order on removal leaves the right foot covered longer, so the right keeps its precedence either way.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
انْتَعَلَأَيْ: أَرَادَ أَحَدُكُمْ لُبْسَ النَّعْلِ
intaʿala — he put on his sandalThat is: one of you intends to put on his sandal.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٢
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا يَمْشِ أَحَدُكُمْ فِي نَعْلٍ وَاحِدَةٍ؛ لِيُنْعِلْهُمَا جَمِيعاً، أَوْ لِيَخْلَعْهُمَا جَمِيعاً»

✎Added by us

“Let none of you walk in one sandal. Let him put both on, or take both off.”

EstablishesWalking in a single sandal is not allowed; either both feet are shod or both are bare.

Lā yamshi aḥadukum fī naʿlin wāḥidah; li-yunʿilhumā jamīʿan, aw li-yakhlaʿhumā jamīʿan

لَاlet not
يَمْشِwalk
أَحَدُكُمْany of you
فِيin
نَعْلٍa sandal
وَاحِدَةٍsingle
لِيُنْعِلْهُمَاlet him put both on
جَمِيعاًtogether
أَوْor
لِيَخْلَعْهُمَاlet him take both off
جَمِيعاًtogether
لَا يَمْشِ أَحَدُكُمْ فِي نَعْلٍ وَاحِدَةٍ
Lā yamshi aḥadukum fī naʿlin wāḥidah
Walking with one foot shod and one bare is ruled out.
وَاحِدَةٍ — root و ح د. Wāḥidah is “one”. The prohibition turns on that word: the fault is the mismatch between the two feet.
لِيُنْعِلْهُمَا جَمِيعاً، أَوْ لِيَخْلَعْهُمَا جَمِيعاً
li-yunʿilhumā jamīʿan, aw li-yakhlaʿhumā jamīʿan
Two acceptable options are given, and both keep the feet matched.
جَمِيعاً — root ج م ع. Jamīʿ is all together. It is repeated for each option, so either state is fine as long as the pair agrees.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

وُجُوبُ إِعْفَاءِ اللِّحَى

Chapter 98 — The Obligation of Letting the Beard Grow

Book p.202 · اللِّبَاسُ وَالهَيْئَةُ — Dress & Appearance · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«خَالِفُوا المُشْرِكِينَ؛ وَفِّرُوا اللِّحَى، وَأَحْفُوا الشَّوَارِبَ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Be unlike the idolaters: let the beards grow full, and cut the moustaches close.”

EstablishesA Muslim man leaves his beard to grow and trims his moustache close, unlike the idolaters.

Khālifū-l-mushrikīn; waffirū-l-liḥā, wa-aḥfū-sh-shawārib

خَالِفُواbe unlike
المُشْرِكِينَthe idolaters
وَفِّرُواleave full
اللِّحَىthe beards
وَأَحْفُواand cut close
الشَّوَارِبَthe moustaches
خَالِفُوا المُشْرِكِينَ
Khālifū-l-mushrikīn
The instruction is to look unlike those who worship other than Allāh.
خَالِفُوا — root خ ل ف. Khālifū is a command to differ, and it is plural: the whole community is addressed, not one man.
وَفِّرُوا اللِّحَى
waffirū-l-liḥā
Leave the beard alone and let it reach its own full length.
وَفِّرُوا — root و ف ر. Tawfīr means leaving a thing abundant. The author glosses it plainly: leave it full, do not cut it back.
وَأَحْفُوا الشَّوَارِبَ
wa-aḥfū-sh-shawārib
Take the moustache down close, so it no longer hangs over the lip.
الشَّوَارِبَ — root ش ر ب. The author explains the order: remove the part of the moustache that comes down onto the lip.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
وَفِّرُواوَفِّرُوا: مِنَ التَّوْفِيرِ، وَهُوَ: الإِبْقَاءُ، أَيِ: اتْرُكُوهَا وَافِرَةً.
waffirū — let them grow fullWaffirū: from al-tawfīr, which is leaving [a thing] intact; that is: leave them full.
الشَّوَارِبَأَيْ: أَزِيلُوا مِنْهَا مَا نَزَلَ عَلَى الشَّفَةِ.
al-shawārib — the moustachesThat is: remove from them whatever comes down over the lip.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

Chapter 99 — Shaving the Head in Patches

Book p.203 · اللِّبَاسُ وَالهَيْئَةُ — Dress & Appearance · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
القَزَعُḤadīth
الكِتَابFrom the book

«نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ عَنِ القَزَعِ»

✎Added by us

“The Prophet ﷺ forbade al-qazaʿ.”

EstablishesHair is not shaved in patches, some of it taken off and some of it left.

Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ ʿani-l-qazaʿ

نَهَىforbade
النَّبِيُّthe Prophet
عَنِagainst
القَزَعِal-qazaʿ
نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ
Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ
This is a prohibition, reported as an act of the Prophet ﷺ forbidding something.
نَهَى — root ن ه ي. Nahā is to forbid. When a Companion reports a nahy without more detail, the wording still carries the force of a ban.
عَنِ القَزَعِ
ʿani-l-qazaʿ
The thing forbidden is a patchy haircut rather than an even one.
القَزَعِ — root ق ز ع. The author defines qazaʿ: shaving off part of the hair and leaving part of it.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
القَزَعِوَهُوَ: حَلْقُ بَعْضِ الشَّعَرِ، وَتَرْكُ بَعْضِهِ.
al-qazaʿ — shaving part of the headAnd it is: shaving some of the hair and leaving some of it.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

الوَصْلُ وَالوَشْمُ وَالنَّمْصُ

Chapter 100 — Hair Extensions, Tattooing, and Plucking the Brows

Book p.204 · اللِّبَاسُ وَالهَيْئَةُ — Dress & Appearance · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَعَنَ اللَّهُ الوَاصِلَةَ وَالمُسْتَوْصِلَةَ، وَالوَاشِمَةَ وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَةَ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allāh has cursed the woman who joins hair on and the woman who has it joined on, and the woman who tattoos and the woman who has herself tattooed.”

EstablishesJoining hair on and tattooing are cursed, and so is asking another person to do either one.

Laʿana-llāhu-l-wāṣilata wa-l-mustawṣilah, wa-l-wāshimata wa-l-mustawshimah

لَعَنَcursed
اللَّهُAllāh
الوَاصِلَةَthe woman who joins hair on
وَالمُسْتَوْصِلَةَand the one who asks for it
وَالوَاشِمَةَand the woman who tattoos
وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَةَand the one who asks for it
لَعَنَ اللَّهُ
Laʿana-llāh
The verdict comes from Allāh Himself, not from taste or custom.
لَعَنَ — root ل ع ن. Laʿn is being cut off from mercy. It is the heaviest word of censure in the language of revelation.
الوَاصِلَةَ وَالمُسْتَوْصِلَةَ
al-wāṣilata wa-l-mustawṣilah
Both the woman doing the work and the woman paying for it are named.
وَالمُسْتَوْصِلَةَ — root و ص ل. The author explains: the wāṣilah is the worker who joins a woman's hair to other hair, wigs and false lashes included; the mustawṣilah is the one who asks for it.
وَالوَاشِمَةَ وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَةَ
wa-l-wāshimata wa-l-mustawshimah
The same pairing again, this time for tattooing.
وَالوَاشِمَةَ — root و ش م. The author describes the wašm: a needle driven into the skin, then the spot packed with a dye that stains it, and it never comes off.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
الوَصْلُالوَصْلُ: وَصْلُ الشَّعَرِ بِشَعَرٍ آخَرَ، وَيَدْخُلُ فِيهِ: وَصْلُ الشَّعَرِ الصِّنَاعِيِّ - المَعْرُوفِ بِـ«البَارُوكَةِ» -، وَالرُّمُوشِ الاِصْطِنَاعِيَّةِ. وَالوَاصِلَةُ: هِيَ العَامِلَةُ الَّتِي تَصِلُ شَعَرَ المَرْأَةِ بِشَعَرٍ آخَرَ. وَالمُسْتَوْصِلَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَطْلُبُ الوَصْلَ.
al-waṣl — joining hair to other hairAl-waṣl: joining hair to other hair. Included in it is joining artificial hair, known as a wig, and artificial eyelashes. And al-wāṣilah: the female practitioner who joins a woman's hair to other hair. And al-mustawṣilah: the woman who asks for the joining.
الوَشْمُالوَشْمُ: غَرْزُ إِبْرَةٍ فِي الجِلْدِ، ثُمَّ حَشْوُ المَوْضِعِ بِمَادَّةٍ يَتَلَوَّنُ مِنْهَا الجِلْدُ إِلَى اللَّوْنِ الأَخْضَرِ الفَاتِحِ، وَلَا يَزُولُ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَبَداً. وَالوَاشِمَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَفْعَلُ الوَشْمَ. وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَطْلُبُ الوَشْمَ.
al-washm — tattooingAl-washm: pricking a needle into the skin, then filling the spot with a substance from which the skin is coloured to a light green, and it never goes away after that. And al-wāshimah: the woman who does the tattooing. And al-mustawshimah: the woman who asks for the tattooing.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٢
قَالَ ابْنُ مَسْعُودٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُIbn Masʿūd (may Allāh be pleased with him) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَعَنَ اللَّهُ الوَاشِمَاتِ وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَاتِ، وَالنَّامِصَاتِ وَالمُتَنَمِّصَاتِ، وَالمُتَفَلِّجَاتِ لِلْحُسْنِ، المُغَيِّرَاتِ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ. وَمَا لِي لَا أَلْعَنُ مَنْ لَعَنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ؟!»

✎Added by us

Ibn Masʿūd, may Allāh be pleased with him, said: “Allāh has cursed the women who tattoo and those who have themselves tattooed, the women who pluck the brows and those who have them plucked, and the women who file their teeth apart for beauty: those who alter the creation of Allāh. And why should I not curse the one whom the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ cursed?”

EstablishesAltering the body for beauty is cursed, and a believer holds the same view the Prophet ﷺ held.

Laʿana-llāhu-l-wāshimāti wa-l-mustawshimāt, wa-n-nāmiṣāti wa-l-mutanammiṣāt, wa-l-mutafallijāti li-l-ḥusn, al-mughayyirāti khalqa-llāh. Wa-mā lī lā alʿanu man laʿana Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ?!

لَعَنَcursed
اللَّهُAllāh
الوَاشِمَاتِthe women who tattoo
وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَاتِand those who ask for it
وَالنَّامِصَاتِand the women who pluck the brows
وَالمُتَنَمِّصَاتِand those who ask for it
وَالمُتَفَلِّجَاتِand the women who file gaps in their teeth
لِلْحُسْنِfor beauty
المُغَيِّرَاتِthe ones who alter
خَلْقَthe creation of
اللَّهِAllāh
وَمَاand why
لِيshould I
لَاnot
أَلْعَنُcurse
مَنْthe one whom
لَعَنَcursed
رَسُولُ اللَّهِthe Messenger of Allāh
لَعَنَ اللَّهُ
Laʿana-llāh
Ibn Masʿūd reports the curse as coming from Allāh, then stands behind it himself.
لَعَنَ — root ل ع ن. He does not soften the verb. Naming a thing cursed is a report, not an insult.
الوَاشِمَاتِ وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَاتِ
al-wāshimāti wa-l-mustawshimāt
Tattooing, and paying to be tattooed, come first in the list.
وَالمُسْتَوْشِمَاتِ — root و ش م with the form of seeking (istafʿala): the mustawshimah is the one who goes and asks for the tattoo.
وَالنَّامِصَاتِ وَالمُتَنَمِّصَاتِ، وَالمُتَفَلِّجَاتِ لِلْحُسْنِ
wa-n-nāmiṣāti wa-l-mutanammiṣāt, wa-l-mutafallijāti li-l-ḥusn
Two more practices: plucking the eyebrows, and filing the teeth to open gaps.
وَالمُتَفَلِّجَاتِ — root ف ل ج. The author explains: the mutafallijah files between her teeth to separate them. The words li-l-ḥusn, 'for beauty', name the motive.
المُغَيِّرَاتِ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ
al-mughayyirāti khalqa-llāh
One phrase gathers all four practices: they change what Allāh made.
المُغَيِّرَاتِ — root غ ي ر. The author reads this as the reason for the curse: altering Allāh's creation by joining hair, tattooing, plucking, and filing for beauty.
وَمَا لِي لَا أَلْعَنُ مَنْ لَعَنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ
Wa-mā lī lā alʿanu man laʿana Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ
Ibn Masʿūd answers an objection: he curses only whom the Prophet ﷺ cursed.
أَلْعَنُ — root ل ع ن. The first-person alʿanu shows a Companion aligning his own tongue with the Prophet's ﷺ ruling, and nothing beyond it.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
النَّامِصَاتِالنَّامِصَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَنْتِفُ شَعَرَ الحَاجِبِ. وَالمُتَنَمِّصَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَطْلُبُ النَّمْصَ.
al-nāmiṣāt — the women who pluck the eyebrowsAl-nāmiṣah: the woman who plucks the hair of the eyebrow. And al-mutanammiṣah: the woman who asks for the plucking.
المُتَفَلِّجَاتِالمُتَفَلِّجَةُ: هِيَ الَّتِي تَبْرُدُ مَا بَيْنَ أَسْنَانِهَا؛ لِتُفَرِّقَهَا عَنْ بَعْضٍ.
al-mutafallijāt — the women who file gaps between the teethAl-mutafallijah: the woman who files what is between her teeth in order to separate them from one another.
المُغَيِّرَاتِ خَلْقَ اللَّهِأَيِ: المُغَيِّرَاتِ خَلْقَ اللَّهِ بِالوَصْلِ، وَالوَشْمِ، وَالنَّمْصِ، وَالتَّفَلُّجِ لِلْحُسْنِ.
al-mughayyirāt khalq Allāh — the women who alter Allāh's creationThat is: those who alter Allāh's creation by joining hair, tattooing, plucking the eyebrows, and filing gaps between the teeth for the sake of beauty.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

«١٠١» · Dress & Appearance

التَّشَبُّهُ

Chapter 101 — Imitating Others

Book p.206 · اللِّبَاسُ وَالهَيْئَةُ — Dress & Appearance · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَنْ تَشَبَّهَ بِقَوْمٍ؛ فَهُوَ مِنْهُمْ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever imitates a people is one of them.”

EstablishesCopying a people's distinctive look and way places you with them, whatever you say you believe.

Man tashabbaha bi-qawmin; fa-huwa minhum

مَنْwhoever
تَشَبَّهَimitates
بِقَوْمٍa people
فَهُوَthen he is
مِنْهُمْof them
مَنْ تَشَبَّهَ بِقَوْمٍ
Man tashabbaha bi-qawmin
Anyone at all who takes on the look and manner of a group.
تَشَبَّهَ — root ش ب ه. Tashabbaha is form V: to make oneself resemble something on purpose. Accidental likeness is not what is meant.
فَهُوَ مِنْهُمْ
fa-huwa minhum
The verdict is short and blunt: he is counted with them.
مِنْهُمْ — root — the particle min of belonging. He is not merely like them; he is reckoned as part of them.

رَوَاهُ أَبُو دَاوُدَReported by Abū Dāwūd

٢
عَنِ ابْنِ عَبَّاسٍ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُمَا قَالَIbn ʿAbbās (may Allāh be pleased with them both) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَعَنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ المُتَشَبِّهِينَ مِنَ الرِّجَالِ بِالنِّسَاءِ، وَالمُتَشَبِّهَاتِ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ بِالرِّجَالِ»

✎Added by us

On the authority of Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allāh be pleased with them both, who said: “The Messenger of Allāh ﷺ cursed the men who imitate women and the women who imitate men.”

EstablishesA man must not take on a woman's appearance or manner, nor a woman a man's.

Laʿana Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ al-mutashabbihīna mina-r-rijāli bi-n-nisāʾ, wa-l-mutashabbihāti mina-n-nisāʾi bi-r-rijāl

لَعَنَcursed
رَسُولُ اللَّهِthe Messenger of Allāh
المُتَشَبِّهِينَthose who imitate
مِنَfrom among
الرِّجَالِthe men
بِالنِّسَاءِwomen
وَالمُتَشَبِّهَاتِand those who imitate
مِنَfrom among
النِّسَاءِthe women
بِالرِّجَالِmen
لَعَنَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ
Laʿana Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ
The curse here is spoken by the Prophet ﷺ himself.
لَعَنَ — root ل ع ن. The subject of the verb is the Messenger ﷺ. Ibn ʿAbbās is reporting words, not offering an opinion.
المُتَشَبِّهِينَ مِنَ الرِّجَالِ بِالنِّسَاءِ
al-mutashabbihīna mina-r-rijāli bi-n-nisāʾ
Men who make themselves resemble women in look, dress, or manner.
المُتَشَبِّهِينَ — root ش ب ه. The active participle names an ongoing habit, not a single slip.
وَالمُتَشَبِّهَاتِ مِنَ النِّسَاءِ بِالرِّجَالِ
wa-l-mutashabbihāti mina-n-nisāʾi bi-r-rijāl
And the same in reverse: women who make themselves resemble men.
وَالمُتَشَبِّهَاتِ — root ش ب ه. The ruling runs both ways, in the same words. Neither side is treated more lightly than the other.

Chapter 102 — Manners of Eating

Book p.208 · آدَابُ الأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ — Eating & Drinking · 4 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«يَا غُلَامُ، سَمِّ اللَّهَ، وَكُلْ بِيَمِينِكَ، وَكُلْ مِمَّا يَلِيكَ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Young man, mention the name of Allāh, eat with your right hand, and eat from what is nearest you.”

EstablishesName Allāh before eating, eat with the right hand, and take from the food closest to you.

Yā ghulām, sammi-llāh, wa-kul bi-yamīnik, wa-kul mimmā yalīk

يَاO
غُلَامُyoung man
سَمِّname
اللَّهَAllāh
وَكُلْand eat
بِيَمِينِكَwith your right hand
وَكُلْand eat
مِمَّاfrom what
يَلِيكَis nearest you
يَا غُلَامُ
Yā ghulām
The Prophet ﷺ corrects a boy at the table, gently and by name of age.
غُلَامُ — root غ ل م. A ghulām is a young lad. Table manners are taught early, and taught kindly.
سَمِّ اللَّهَ
sammi-llāh
Begin by putting the name of Allāh on the food.
سَمِّ — root س م و. Sammi is 'name': say bismi-llāh. The first act of eating is a word, not a bite.
وَكُلْ بِيَمِينِكَ
wa-kul bi-yamīnik
The right hand is the eating hand.
بِيَمِينِكَ — root ي م ن. Yamīn is the right hand, and in the language it carries the sense of blessing and of the better side.
وَكُلْ مِمَّا يَلِيكَ
wa-kul mimmā yalīk
Take from the part of the dish in front of you, not from across it.
يَلِيكَ — root و ل ي. Yalīka is what adjoins you. Reaching over a shared dish is what the wording rules out.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٢
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«كُلُوا فِي القَصْعَةِ مِنْ جَوَانِبِهَا، وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا مِنْ وَسَطِهَا؛ فَإِنَّ البَرَكَةَ تَنْزِلُ فِي وَسَطِهَا»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Eat from the sides of the large dish, and do not eat from its middle, for the blessing comes down in its middle.”

EstablishesEat from the edges of a shared dish and leave the centre alone, where the blessing settles.

Kulū fī-l-qaṣʿati min jawānibihā, wa-lā taʾkulū min wasaṭihā; fa-inna-l-barakata tanzilu fī wasaṭihā

كُلُواeat
فِيin
القَصْعَةِthe large dish
مِنْfrom
جَوَانِبِهَاits sides
وَلَاand do not
تَأْكُلُواeat
مِنْfrom
وَسَطِهَاits middle
فَإِنَّfor indeed
البَرَكَةَthe blessing
تَنْزِلُcomes down
فِيin
وَسَطِهَاits middle
كُلُوا فِي القَصْعَةِ مِنْ جَوَانِبِهَا
Kulū fī-l-qaṣʿati min jawānibihā
With a big shared dish, everyone works inward from the rim.
القَصْعَةِ — root ق ص ع. The author defines the qaṣʿah: a wide open dish that feeds ten people. The manner assumes a communal meal.
وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا مِنْ وَسَطِهَا
wa-lā taʾkulū min wasaṭihā
The middle is left untouched while the sides are still full.
وَسَطِهَا — root و س ط. Wasaṭ is the exact centre. The prohibition is about where you start, not about how much you eat.
فَإِنَّ البَرَكَةَ تَنْزِلُ فِي وَسَطِهَا
fa-inna-l-barakata tanzilu fī wasaṭihā
The reason is given openly: blessing descends into the centre.
تَنْزِلُ — root ن ز ل. Tanzilu is 'comes down', from above. The blessing is placed in the food, not produced by it.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
القَصْعَةِالقَصْعَةُ: إِنَاءٌ مَبْسُوطٌ يُشْبِعُ عَشَرَةَ أَنْفُسٍ.
al-qaṣʿah — a wide bowlAl-qaṣʿah: a wide vessel that satisfies ten persons.

رَوَاهُ أَحْمَدُReported by Aḥmad

٣
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا وَقَعَتْ لُقْمَةُ أَحَدِكُمْ فَلْيَأْخُذْهَا، فَلْيُمِطْ مَا كَانَ بِهَا مِنْ أَذىً، وَلْيَأْكُلْهَا، وَلَا يَدَعْهَا لِلشَّيْطَانِ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “When a morsel of any of you falls, let him pick it up, remove whatever harm is on it, and eat it. Let him not leave it for the devil.”

EstablishesA dropped morsel is cleaned and eaten, not discarded; throwing food away hands it to the devil.

Idhā waqaʿat luqmatu aḥadikum fa-l-yaʾkhudhhā, fa-l-yumiṭ mā kāna bihā min adhan, wa-l-yaʾkulhā, wa-lā yadaʿhā li-sh-shayṭān

إِذَاwhen
وَقَعَتْfalls
لُقْمَةُthe morsel of
أَحَدِكُمْone of you
فَلْيَأْخُذْهَاthen let him take it
فَلْيُمِطْlet him remove
مَاwhatever
كَانَwas
بِهَاon it
مِنْof
أَذىًdirt
وَلْيَأْكُلْهَاand let him eat it
وَلَاand let him not
يَدَعْهَاleave it
لِلشَّيْطَانِfor the devil
إِذَا وَقَعَتْ لُقْمَةُ أَحَدِكُمْ
Idhā waqaʿat luqmatu aḥadikum
The case is ordinary: a mouthful slips and lands on the ground.
لُقْمَةُ — root ل ق م. A luqmah is one mouthful, the smallest unit of a meal. Even that much is worth this ruling.
فَلْيَأْخُذْهَا، فَلْيُمِطْ مَا كَانَ بِهَا مِنْ أَذىً، وَلْيَأْكُلْهَا
fa-l-yaʾkhudhhā, fa-l-yumiṭ mā kāna bihā min adhan, wa-l-yaʾkulhā
Three commands in order: pick it up, clean it, eat it.
فَلْيُمِطْ — root م ي ط. The author glosses fa-l-yumiṭ as 'let him remove'. Clean the morsel; do not clean the floor of it into the bin.
وَلَا يَدَعْهَا لِلشَّيْطَانِ
wa-lā yadaʿhā li-sh-shayṭān
Food abandoned on the ground is described as left to the devil.
يَدَعْهَا — root و د ع. Yadaʿ is to leave a thing behind. The wording makes waste a transfer, not just a loss.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
فَلْيُمِطْأَيْ: فَلْيُزِلْ.
fal-yumiṭ — let him remove itThat is: let him take it away.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

٤
عَنْ أَبِي هُرَيْرَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ قَالَAbū Hurayrah (may Allāh be pleased with him) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَا عَابَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ طَعَاماً قَطُّ؛ إِنِ اشْتَهَاهُ أَكَلَهُ، وَإِنْ كَرِهَهُ تَرَكَهُ»

✎Added by us

Abū Hurayrah, may Allāh be pleased with him, said: “The Messenger of Allāh ﷺ never found fault with food. If he had an appetite for it he ate it, and if he disliked it he left it.”

EstablishesNever criticise food. Eat what you have appetite for and leave the rest without comment.

Mā ʿāba Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ ṭaʿāman qaṭṭ; ini-shtahāhu akalah, wa-in karihahu tarakah

مَاnever
عَابَfound fault with
رَسُولُ اللَّهِthe Messenger of Allāh
طَعَاماًany food
قَطُّever
إِنِif
اشْتَهَاهُhe desired it
أَكَلَهُhe ate it
وَإِنْand if
كَرِهَهُhe disliked it
تَرَكَهُhe left it
مَا عَابَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ طَعَاماً قَطُّ
Mā ʿāba Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ ṭaʿāman qaṭṭ
In a whole lifetime he is not recorded criticising a single dish.
عَابَ — root ع ي ب. ʿAyb is a defect; ʿāba is to point one out. With mā and qaṭṭ the denial covers all of his life, without exception.
إِنِ اشْتَهَاهُ أَكَلَهُ
ini-shtahāhu akalah
Appetite was reason enough to eat.
اشْتَهَاهُ — root ش ه و. Shahwah is plain appetite. Wanting the food is treated as a sufficient reason, needing no praise of the cook.
وَإِنْ كَرِهَهُ تَرَكَهُ
wa-in karihahu tarakah
Dislike was met with silence, not with a remark.
تَرَكَهُ — root ت ر ك. Tarakahu is simply 'he left it'. The alternative to eating is leaving, not complaining.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

آدَابُ الشُّرْبِ

Chapter 103 — Manners of Drinking

Book p.210 · آدَابُ الأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ — Eating & Drinking · 4 entries in the printed text.

١
آدَابُ الشُّرْبِḤadīth
الكِتَابFrom the book

«نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ عَنِ الشُّرْبِ قَائِماً»

✎Added by us

“The Prophet ﷺ forbade drinking while standing.”

EstablishesSit down to drink; drinking on your feet was forbidden by the Prophet ﷺ.

Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ ʿani-sh-shurbi qāʾiman

نَهَىforbade
النَّبِيُّthe Prophet
عَنِagainst
الشُّرْبِdrinking
قَائِماًstanding
نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ
Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ
A prohibition, reported as an act of his.
نَهَى — root ن ه ي. Nahy is a ban. The reporter gives the ruling without the occasion.
عَنِ الشُّرْبِ قَائِماً
ʿani-sh-shurbi qāʾiman
What is forbidden is not the drink but the posture.
قَائِماً — root ق و م. Qāʾiman is a ḥāl, a word describing the state of the drinker: on his feet. Sitting is the manner intended.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

٢
آدَابُ الشُّرْبِḤadīth
الكِتَابFrom the book

«نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ عَنِ النَّفْخِ فِي الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ»

✎Added by us

“The Prophet ﷺ forbade blowing into food and drink.”

EstablishesDo not blow on food or drink to cool it; let it cool by itself.

Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ ʿani-n-nafkhi fī-ṭ-ṭaʿāmi wa-sh-sharāb

نَهَىforbade
النَّبِيُّthe Prophet
عَنِagainst
النَّفْخِblowing
فِيinto
الطَّعَامِfood
وَالشَّرَابِand drink
نَهَى النَّبِيُّ ﷺ
Nahā-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ
Another reported prohibition, in the same short form.
النَّبِيُّ — root ن ب أ. Nabī is one who brings news from Allāh. A ban from him is not a matter of etiquette or preference.
عَنِ النَّفْخِ
ʿani-n-nafkhi
The act named is breathing out hard onto something.
النَّفْخِ — root ن ف خ. Nafkh is a forceful breath. It carries what is in the mouth onto the food.
فِي الطَّعَامِ وَالشَّرَابِ
fī-ṭ-ṭaʿāmi wa-sh-sharāb
Both solids and liquids are covered.
وَالشَّرَابِ — root ش ر ب. Sharāb is anything drunk. Naming food and drink together closes the gap someone might argue for.

رَوَاهُ أَحْمَدُReported by Aḥmad

٣
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا شَرِبَ أَحَدُكُمْ؛ فَلَا يَتَنَفَّسْ فِي الإِنَاءِ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “When one of you drinks, let him not breathe into the vessel.”

EstablishesBreathe outside the cup, never into it, while you are drinking.

Idhā shariba aḥadukum; fa-lā yatanaffas fī-l-ināʾ

إِذَاwhen
شَرِبَdrinks
أَحَدُكُمْone of you
فَلَاthen let him not
يَتَنَفَّسْbreathe
فِيinto
الإِنَاءِthe vessel
إِذَا شَرِبَ أَحَدُكُمْ
Idhā shariba aḥadukum
The setting is any ordinary drink by any ordinary person.
أَحَدُكُمْ — root أ ح د. Aḥadukum, 'one of you', is how the Prophet ﷺ addresses a manner meant for everyone.
فَلَا يَتَنَفَّسْ فِي الإِنَاءِ
fa-lā yatanaffas fī-l-ināʾ
The breath must go somewhere other than the cup.
يَتَنَفَّسْ — root ن ف س. Tanaffasa is form V: to draw and let out breath. Only the direction is forbidden, not the breathing.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٤
آدَابُ الشُّرْبِḤadīth
الكِتَابFrom the book

«كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ يَتَنَفَّسُ فِي الشَّرَابِ ثَلَاثاً»

ثَلَاثاًthree times

✎Added by us

“The Prophet ﷺ would take breath three times while drinking.”

EstablishesDrink in three goes, lowering the cup to breathe between them rather than draining it at once.

Kāna-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ yatanaffasu fī-sh-sharābi thalāthan

كَانَused to
النَّبِيُّthe Prophet
يَتَنَفَّسُtake breath
فِيduring
الشَّرَابِthe drink
ثَلَاثاًthree times
كَانَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺ
Kāna-n-Nabiyyu ﷺ
Kāna with a present verb reports a settled habit, not a single occasion.
كَانَ — root ك و ن. Kāna followed by yatanaffasu means 'he used to', which is how the Companions described his regular practice.
يَتَنَفَّسُ فِي الشَّرَابِ ثَلَاثاً
yatanaffasu fī-sh-sharābi thalāthan
He drank in three stages, breathing between them.
ثَلَاثاً — root ث ل ث. The author is careful here: the three breaths are taken outside the vessel. Read with the previous hadith, the two fit together.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
ثَلَاثاًأَيْ: إِذَا شَرِبَ يَتَنَفَّسُ خَارِجَ الإِنَاءِ ثَلَاثاً.
thalāthan — three timesThat is: when he drinks he breathes outside the vessel three times.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

«١٠٤» · Eating & Drinking

الفَرَاغُ مِنَ الأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ

Chapter 104 — Finishing a Meal or a Drink

Book p.212 · آدَابُ الأَكْلِ وَالشُّرْبِ — Eating & Drinking · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
أَمَرَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ بِلَعْقِ الأَصَابِعِ وَالصَّحْفَةِ، وَقَالَThe Messenger of Allāh ﷺ ordered that the fingers and the plate be licked, and said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِنَّكُمْ لَا تَدْرُونَ فِي أَيِّهِ البَرَكَةُ»

✎Added by us

The Messenger of Allāh ﷺ ordered that the fingers and the dish be licked clean, and said: “You do not know in which of them the blessing lies.”

EstablishesWipe the dish and fingers clean; the blessing may sit in the part you would have discarded.

Innakum lā tadrūna fī ayyihi-l-barakah

إِنَّكُمْindeed you
لَاdo not
تَدْرُونَknow
فِيin
أَيِّهِwhich of it
البَرَكَةُthe blessing is
إِنَّكُمْ لَا تَدْرُونَ
Innakum lā tadrūna
The reason for the order is our own ignorance.
تَدْرُونَ — root د ر ي. Dirāyah is knowing a thing by looking into it. We cannot see where the blessing sits, so we leave nothing behind.
فِي أَيِّهِ البَرَكَةُ
fī ayyihi-l-barakah
The blessing could be in any part of the meal, including the last smear.
البَرَكَةُ — root ب ر ك. Barakah is good that increases and stays. Since it is not visible, no portion of the food can be written off.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
بِلَعْقِ الأَصَابِعِ وَالصَّحْفَةِأَيْ: مَسْحُ مَا عَلَى الإِنَاءِ مِنْ أَثَرِ الطَّعَامِ بِالأَصَابِعِ، ثُمَّ مَصُّ أَصَابِعِهِ. وَالصَّحْفَةُ: إِنَاءٌ مَبْسُوطٌ يُشْبِعُ خَمْسَةَ أَنْفُسٍ.
bi-laʿq al-aṣābiʿ wa-l-ṣaḥfah — licking the fingers and the dishThat is: wiping off what is on the vessel of the traces of food with the fingers, then sucking his fingers. And al-ṣaḥfah: a wide vessel that satisfies five persons.

رَوَاهُ مُسْلِمٌReported by Muslim

٢
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِنَّ اللَّهَ لَيَرْضَى عَنِ العَبْدِ؛ أَنْ يَأْكُلَ الأَكْلَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا. أَوْ يَشْرَبَ الشَّرْبَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Allāh is truly pleased with the servant who eats a meal and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it.”

EstablishesPraising Allāh after eating or drinking earns His pleasure, for an act that costs almost nothing.

Inna-llāha la-yarḍā ʿani-l-ʿabd; an yaʾkula-l-aklata fa-yaḥmadahu ʿalayhā. Aw yashraba-sh-sharbata fa-yaḥmadahu ʿalayhā

The reward named is the pleasure of Allāh Himself.
لَيَرْضَى — root ر ض و. Riḍā is being pleased with someone. The inna and the lām both strengthen it: this really does please Him.
أَنْ يَأْكُلَ الأَكْلَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا

One meal, followed by a word of praise.
فَيَحْمَدَهُ — root ح م د. Ḥamd is praise given because the one praised deserves it. The fa- makes it follow straight after the eating.
أَوْ يَشْرَبَ الشَّرْبَةَ فَيَحْمَدَهُ عَلَيْهَا
aw yashraba-sh-sharbata fa-yaḥmadahu ʿalayhā
The same again for a single drink of water.
الشَّرْبَةَ — root ش ر ب. Sharbah is one drink, not a habit of drinking. The smallness of the act is the point of the hadith.

Chapter 105 — The Road

Book p.214 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«الإِيمَانُ بِضْعٌ وَسَبْعُونَ - أَوْ: بِضْعٌ وَسِتُّونَ - شُعْبَةً. فَأَفْضَلُهَا: قَوْلُ: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ. وَأَدْنَاهَا: إِمَاطَةُ الأَذَى عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ. وَالحَيَاءُ شُعْبَةٌ مِنَ الإِيمَانِ»

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْSay it: this is named the highest branch of faith.
لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Faith is some seventy, or some sixty, branches. The highest of them is saying, ‘There is no god but Allāh,’ and the lowest of them is clearing harm off the road. And modesty is a branch of faith.”

EstablishesFaith has many branches, from the testimony at the top to clearing harm off the road.

Al-īmānu biḍʿun wa-sabʿūn — aw: biḍʿun wa-sittūn — shuʿbah. Fa-afḍaluhā: qawlu: Lā ilāha illa-llāh. Wa-adnāhā: imāṭatu-l-adhā ʿani-ṭ-ṭarīq. Wa-l-ḥayāʾu shuʿbatun mina-l-īmān

Al-īmānu biḍʿun wa-sabʿūn — aw: biḍʿun wa-sittūn — shuʿbah
Faith is not one thing but many parts, counted in the sixties or seventies.
بِضْعٌ — root ب ض ع. The author defines biḍʿ as a number between three and nine, so this is 'sixty-something' or 'seventy-something'. Shuʿbah he glosses as a trait or quality.
فَأَفْضَلُهَا: قَوْلُ: لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
Fa-afḍaluhā: qawlu: Lā ilāha illa-llāh
At the top of the range stands the testimony that Allāh alone is God.
قَوْلُ — root ق و ل. It is qawl, speech: a sentence said and meant. The highest branch of faith is something you can begin doing now.
وَأَدْنَاهَا: إِمَاطَةُ الأَذَى عَنِ الطَّرِيقِ
Wa-adnāhā: imāṭatu-l-adhā ʿani-ṭ-ṭarīq
At the bottom of the range: moving something harmful out of people's way.
إِمَاطَةُ — root م ي ط. Imāṭah is removal. Calling it the lowest branch still calls it faith, which is why the road is a place of worship.
وَالحَيَاءُ شُعْبَةٌ مِنَ الإِيمَانِ
Wa-l-ḥayāʾu shuʿbatun mina-l-īmān
Modesty is named as one of these branches by itself.
وَالحَيَاءُ — root ح ي ي. Ḥayāʾ is the restraint that holds a person back from what is ugly. Here it is not merely a good manner; it is part of faith.

٢
عَنْ أَبِي سَعِيدٍ الخُدْرِيِّ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُ أَنَّ النَّبِيَّ ﷺ قَالَFrom Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī (may Allāh be pleased with him) that the Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِيَّاكُمْ وَالجُلُوسَ بِالطُّرُقَاتِ. قَالُوا: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، مَا لَنَا بُدٌّ مِنْ مَجَالِسِنَا؛ نَتَحَدَّثُ فِيهَا. قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: إِذَا أَبَيْتُمْ إِلَّا المَجْلِسَ؛ فَأَعْطُوا الطَّرِيقَ حَقَّهُ. قَالُوا: وَمَا حَقُّهُ؟ قَالَ: غَضُّ البَصَرِ، وَكَفُّ الأَذَى، وَرَدُّ السَّلَامِ، وَالأَمْرُ بِالمَعْرُوفِ، وَالنَّهْيُ عَنِ المُنْكَرِ»

✎Added by us

On the authority of Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, may Allāh be pleased with him, that the Prophet ﷺ said: “Beware of sitting in the roadways.” They said, “Messenger of Allāh, we cannot do without our sitting places; we talk in them.” The Messenger of Allāh ﷺ said, “If you will not give up the gathering, then give the road its due.” They said, “And what is its due?” He said, “Lowering the gaze, holding back harm, returning the greeting, enjoining what is right, and forbidding what is wrong.”

EstablishesIf you sit where people pass, you owe the road: lowered gaze, no harm, returned greetings, right upheld.

Iyyākum wa-l-julūsa bi-ṭ-ṭuruqāt. Qālū: Yā Rasūla-llāh, mā lanā buddun min majālisinā; nataḥaddathu fīhā. Qāla Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ: Idhā abaytum illa-l-majlis; fa-aʿṭū-ṭ-ṭarīqa ḥaqqah. Qālū: Wa-mā ḥaqquh? Qāla: Ghaḍḍu-l-baṣar, wa-kaffu-l-adhā, wa-raddu-s-salām, wa-l-amru bi-l-maʿrūf, wa-n-nahyu ʿani-l-munkar

إِيَّاكُمْ وَالجُلُوسَ بِالطُّرُقَاتِ
Iyyākum wa-l-julūsa bi-ṭ-ṭuruqāt
The first word is a warning: do not make the roadside your sitting room.
إِيَّاكُمْ — root — iyyākum is a fixed formula of warning, 'keep clear of'. It is stronger than a plain 'do not'.
قَالُوا: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، مَا لَنَا بُدٌّ مِنْ مَجَالِسِنَا؛ نَتَحَدَّثُ فِيهَا
Qālū: Yā Rasūla-llāh, mā lanā buddun min majālisinā; nataḥaddathu fīhā
The Companions answer honestly: these gatherings are part of their life.
بُدٌّ — root ب د د. Lā budda minhu means 'there is no avoiding it'. The author glosses their words: we cannot do without these sittings.
قَالَ رَسُولُ اللَّهِ ﷺ: إِذَا أَبَيْتُمْ إِلَّا المَجْلِسَ
Qāla Rasūlu-llāhi ﷺ: Idhā abaytum illa-l-majlis
He does not repeat the ban. He accepts their situation and sets conditions.
أَبَيْتُمْ — root أ ب ي. Abā is to refuse or decline. The wording concedes their need without pretending the warning was not given.
فَأَعْطُوا الطَّرِيقَ حَقَّهُ
fa-aʿṭū-ṭ-ṭarīqa ḥaqqah
The road is spoken of as having a right you must pay.
حَقَّهُ — root ح ق ق. Ḥaqq is a due that is owed, not a favour. Public space is put on the same footing as a creditor.
قَالُوا: وَمَا حَقُّهُ
Qālū: Wa-mā ḥaqquh?
They ask for the specifics rather than guessing at them.
قَالُوا — root ق و ل. Qālū: they answer back with a question. Asking what a duty actually contains is part of accepting it.
قَالَ: غَضُّ البَصَرِ، وَكَفُّ الأَذَى، وَرَدُّ السَّلَامِ، وَالأَمْرُ بِالمَعْرُوفِ، وَالنَّهْيُ عَنِ المُنْكَرِ
Qāla: Ghaḍḍu-l-baṣar, wa-kaffu-l-adhā, wa-raddu-s-salām, wa-l-amru bi-l-maʿrūf, wa-n-nahyu ʿani-l-munkar
Five duties: two restraints on yourself, then three things you owe the people passing.
غَضُّ — root غ ض ض. Ghaḍḍ is lowering or dropping the gaze, not shutting the eyes. Kaff, root ك ف ف, is holding your hand and tongue back from harming anyone.

majālisinā — our gatheringsThat is: we have no way of doing without these gatherings.

Chapter 106 — The Greeting of Peace

Book p.216 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا تَدْخُلُونَ الجَنَّةَ حَتَّى تُؤْمِنُوا، وَلَا تُؤْمِنُوا حَتَّى تَحَابُّوا. أَوَلَا أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَى شَيْءٍ إِذَا فَعَلْتُمُوهُ تَحَابَبْتُمْ؟ أَفْشُوا السَّلَامَ بَيْنَكُمْ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “You will not enter Paradise until you believe, and you will not believe until you love one another. Shall I not tell you of something which, if you do it, will make you love one another? Spread the greeting of peace among yourselves.”

EstablishesGreeting people with salām openly builds the mutual love that faith, and entry to Paradise, depend on.

Lā tadkhulūna-l-jannata ḥattā tuʾminū, wa-lā tuʾminū ḥattā taḥābbū. A-wa-lā adullukum ʿalā shayʾin idhā faʿaltumūhu taḥābabtum? Afshū-s-salāma baynakum

السَّلَامَthe greeting of peace
بَيْنَكُمْamong yourselves
لَا تَدْخُلُونَ الجَنَّةَ حَتَّى تُؤْمِنُوا
Lā tadkhulūna-l-jannata ḥattā tuʾminū
Paradise waits on faith. Nothing enters without it.
حَتَّى — root — ḥattā is a particle marking a limit that must be reached first. It sets up a chain, each link resting on the next.
وَلَا تُؤْمِنُوا حَتَّى تَحَابُّوا
wa-lā tuʾminū ḥattā taḥābbū
And faith itself waits on love between believers.
تَحَابُّوا — root ح ب ب. Taḥābbū is form VI: loving one another, both ways. A one-sided affection does not answer the wording.
أَوَلَا أَدُلُّكُمْ عَلَى شَيْءٍ إِذَا فَعَلْتُمُوهُ تَحَابَبْتُمْ
A-wa-lā adullukum ʿalā shayʾin idhā faʿaltumūhu taḥābabtum?
He offers a practical way in, and asks before giving it.
أَدُلُّكُمْ — root د ل ل. Dalla is to point the way. He treats them as people who will act on directions, not just hear them.
أَفْشُوا السَّلَامَ بَيْنَكُمْ
Afshū-s-salāma baynakum
The answer is one habit, repeated: greet each other with peace.
أَفْشُوا — root ف ش و. The author glosses afshū: make it visible and spread it among yourselves. Not a private greeting for friends, but an open one for all.

سُئِلَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ was asked
الكِتَابFrom the book

«أَيُّ الإِسْلَامِ خَيْرٌ؟ قَالَ: تُطْعِمُ الطَّعَامَ، وَتَقْرَأُ السَّلَامَ عَلَى مَنْ عَرَفْتَ وَمَنْ لَمْ تَعْرِفْ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ was asked: “Which part of Islam is best?” He said, “That you feed people, and that you give the greeting of peace to those you know and those you do not know.”

EstablishesFeed people and greet everyone, known or unknown; this is named among the best of Islam.

Ayyu-l-Islāmi khayr? Qāla: Tuṭʿimu-ṭ-ṭaʿām, wa-taqraʾu-s-salāma ʿalā man ʿarafta wa-man lam taʿrif

أَيُّ الإِسْلَامِ خَيْرٌ
Ayyu-l-Islāmi khayr?
The question asks which of Islam's practices ranks highest.
خَيْرٌ — root خ ي ر. Khayr here is comparative: better, best. The answer given is two everyday habits, not two rare feats.
قَالَ: تُطْعِمُ الطَّعَامَ
Qāla: Tuṭʿimu-ṭ-ṭaʿām
First answer: put food in front of people.
تُطْعِمُ — root ط ع م. Tuṭʿimu is form IV, to feed someone else. The verb is addressed to you personally, in the singular.
وَتَقْرَأُ السَّلَامَ عَلَى مَنْ عَرَفْتَ وَمَنْ لَمْ تَعْرِفْ
wa-taqraʾu-s-salāma ʿalā man ʿarafta wa-man lam taʿrif
Second answer: greet strangers as readily as friends.
وَتَقْرَأُ — root ق ر أ. Taqraʾu-s-salām is to deliver the greeting aloud. The two clauses that follow remove any filter on who receives it.

الاِسْتِئْذَانُ

Chapter 107 — Asking Permission to Enter

Book p.217 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِنَّمَا جُعِلَ الاِسْتِئْذَانُ مِنْ أَجْلِ البَصَرِ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Permission to enter was made a rule only because of the eye.”

EstablishesAsking permission exists to keep your eyes out of a household's privacy, so never look in first.

Innamā juʿila-l-istiʾdhānu min ajli-l-baṣar

إِنَّمَاonly

الاِسْتِئْذَانُasking permission

إِنَّمَا جُعِلَ الاِسْتِئْذَانُ
Innamā juʿila-l-istiʾdhānu
The rule has one stated purpose, and innamā limits it to that.
الاِسْتِئْذَانُ — root أ ذ ن. Istiʾdhān is form X: seeking permission. Juʿila is passive, so the rule was laid down, not invented by people.
مِنْ أَجْلِ البَصَرِ
min ajli-l-baṣar
The reason is sight: the eye must not get inside before you do.
البَصَرِ — root ب ص ر. The author explains it: permission was legislated so that the gaze does not fall into the inside of the house. Knocking, then standing where you cannot see in, follows from this.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
مِنْ أَجْلِ البَصَرِأَيْ: إِنَّمَا شُرِعَ الاِسْتِئْذَانُ؛ لِئَلَّا يَقَعَ البَصَرُ إِلَى دَاخِلِ البَيْتِ.
min ajl al-baṣar — on account of the gazeThat is: seeking permission was legislated only so that the gaze would not fall upon the inside of the house.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)

٢
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا اسْتَأْذَنَ أَحَدُكُمْ ثَلَاثاً فَلَمْ يُؤْذَنْ لَهُ؛ فَلْيَرْجِعْ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “When one of you asks permission three times and is not given it, let him go back.”

EstablishesAsk at most three times. If no permission comes, leave without pressing or waiting.

Idhā-staʾdhana aḥadukum thalāthan fa-lam yuʾdhan lah; fa-l-yarjiʿ

إِذَاwhen
اسْتَأْذَنَasks permission

ثَلَاثاًthree times
فَلَمْand he is not

لَهُto him

Idhā-staʾdhana aḥadukum thalāthan
Three requests is the limit, not the minimum.
ثَلَاثاً — root ث ل ث. Thalāthan caps the asking. Beyond three, the silence itself is treated as an answer.
فَلَمْ يُؤْذَنْ لَهُ؛ فَلْيَرْجِعْ
fa-lam yuʾdhan lah; fa-l-yarjiʿ
No answer means go home, with no offence taken.
فَلْيَرْجِعْ — root ر ج ع. Yarjiʿ is to return the way you came. The command protects the household's right to decline without saying so.

Chapter 108 — Not Arriving Home at Night Unannounced

Book p.218 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِذَا أَطَالَ أَحَدُكُمُ الغَيْبَةَ؛ فَلَا يَطْرُقْ أَهْلَهُ لَيْلاً»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “When one of you has been away a long time, let him not come upon his family at night.”

EstablishesAfter a long absence, do not arrive on your household at night unless they expect you.

Idhā aṭāla aḥadukumu-l-ghaybah; fa-lā yaṭruq ahlahu laylan

The case is a long trip away from home, not an evening out.
الغَيْبَةَ — root غ ي ب. Ghaybah is absence, being out of sight. The length of it is what creates the problem this hadith addresses.
فَلَا يَطْرُقْ أَهْلَهُ لَيْلاً

Do not turn up unannounced in the dark.
يَطْرُقْ — root ط ر ق. Ṭaraqa is to come knocking at night. The author notes the exception plainly: unless they already know he is arriving.

Chapter 109 — The Gathering

Book p.219 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 3 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا يُقِيمُ الرَّجُلُ الرَّجُلَ مِنْ مَقْعَدِهِ ثُمَّ يَجْلِسُ فِيهِ، وَلَكِنْ تَفَسَّحُوا وَتَوَسَّعُوا»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “No man is to make another man get up from his seat and then sit in it himself. Rather, close up and make room.”

EstablishesNever move someone out of his seat to take it; shift closer together and make space instead.

Lā yuqīmu-r-rajulu-r-rajula min maqʿadihi thumma yajlisu fīh, wa-lākin tafassaḥū wa-tawassaʿū

لَاnot
يُقِيمُshall make stand
الرَّجُلُa man
الرَّجُلَanother man

مَقْعَدِهِhis seat

وَتَوَسَّعُواand make room

Lā yuqīmu-r-rajulu-r-rajula min maqʿadihi
One man does not put another out of the place he is sitting in.
يُقِيمُ — root ق و م. Yuqīmu is form IV: to make someone stand up. Rank, age, and status are not offered as exceptions.
ثُمَّ يَجْلِسُ فِيهِ
thumma yajlisu fīh
The wrong is sharpened by what follows: he takes the seat for himself.
ثُمَّ — root — thumma marks sequence. It names the motive: the seat was wanted, so its occupant was moved.
وَلَكِنْ تَفَسَّحُوا وَتَوَسَّعُوا
wa-lākin tafassaḥū wa-tawassaʿū
The alternative is given: everyone shifts to make the space needed.
تَفَسَّحُوا — root ف س ح. The author explains tafassaḥū: let each of you draw near the other so the gathering opens up. The burden falls on those already seated.
الكِتَابFrom the book
مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses

tafassaḥū — make roomThat is: let each of you draw close to the other, so that the sitting place may make room.

٢
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَنْ قَامَ مِنْ مَجْلِسِهِ ثُمَّ رَجَعَ إِلَيْهِ؛ فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever gets up from his seat and then comes back to it has the better right to it.”

EstablishesA seat still belongs to whoever briefly left it; he has first claim when he returns.

Man qāma min majlisihi thumma rajaʿa ilayh; fa-huwa aḥaqqu bih

The case is a person stepping away from where he was sitting.
مَجْلِسِهِ — root ج ل س. Majlis is both the gathering and the spot you sit in. Here it means the place itself.
ثُمَّ رَجَعَ إِلَيْهِ

He comes back, having meant to return all along.
رَجَعَ — root ر ج ع. Rujūʿ is coming back to a place you left. Leaving for good is a different case and not covered here.
فَهُوَ أَحَقُّ بِهِ
fa-huwa aḥaqqu bih
His claim on that spot outranks the claim of whoever filled it.
أَحَقُّ — root ح ق ق. Aḥaqq is the comparative of ḥaqq: he has the stronger right. This is a rule of entitlement, not a request for courtesy.

٣
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَنِ اسْتَمَعَ إِلَى حَدِيثِ قَوْمٍ وَهُمْ لَهُ كَارِهُونَ - أَوْ: يَفِرُّونَ مِنْهُ -؛ صُبَّ فِي أُذُنِهِ الآنُكُ يَوْمَ القِيَامَةِ»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “Whoever listens in on a people's conversation when they are unwilling for him to hear it, or when they move away from him, molten lead will be poured into his ear on the Day of Resurrection.”

EstablishesDo not listen in on talk not meant for you; eavesdropping carries a punishment in the ear.

Mani-stamaʿa ilā ḥadīthi qawmin wa-hum lahu kārihūn — aw: yafirrūna minh —; ṣubba fī udhunihi-l-ānuku yawma-l-qiyāmah

Mani-stamaʿa ilā ḥadīthi qawmin
Deliberate listening, not overhearing by accident.
اسْتَمَعَ — root س م ع. Istamaʿa is form VIII: to listen on purpose, leaning in. Simple samiʿa, hearing without trying, is not what is described.
وَهُمْ لَهُ كَارِهُونَ - أَوْ: يَفِرُّونَ مِنْهُ
wa-hum lahu kārihūn — aw: yafirrūna minh —
Their unwillingness is what makes the listening wrong.
يَفِرُّونَ — root ف ر ر. The author glosses yafirrūna minhu: they move away from him so he will not hear their talk. Their behaviour is a clear enough signal.
صُبَّ فِي أُذُنِهِ الآنُكُ
ṣubba fī udhunihi-l-ānuku
The punishment lands on the organ that committed the offence.
الآنُكُ — root أ ن ك. The author defines al-ānuk: molten lead. The recompense matches the act, ear for ear.
يَوْمَ القِيَامَةِ
yawma-l-qiyāmah
The account is settled later, not now.
القِيَامَةِ — root ق و م. Qiyāmah is the standing up, when all are raised for judgement. A private sin heard by nobody is still on the record.

Chapter 110 — The One You Sit With

Book p.221 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَثَلُ الجَلِيسِ الصَّالِحِ وَالسَّوْءِ: كَحَامِلِ المِسْكِ وَنَافِخِ الكِيرِ. فَحَامِلُ المِسْكِ: إِمَّا أَنْ يُحْذِيَكَ، وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَبْتَاعَ مِنْهُ، وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَجِدَ مِنْهُ رِيحاً طَيِّبَةً. وَنَافِخُ الكِيرِ: إِمَّا أَنْ يُحْرِقَ ثِيَابَكَ، وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَجِدَ رِيحاً خَبِيثَةً»

✎Added by us

The Prophet ﷺ said: “The likeness of a good companion and a bad one is the carrier of musk and the blower of the bellows. As for the carrier of musk: either he gives you some, or you buy some from him, or you catch a good scent from him. And as for the blower of the bellows: either he burns your clothes, or you catch a foul smell.”

EstablishesChoose your company. A good companion leaves you better off; a bad one burns you or leaves his stink.

Mathalu-l-jalīsi-ṣ-ṣāliḥi wa-s-sawʾ: ka-ḥāmili-l-miski wa-nāfikhi-l-kīr. Fa-ḥāmilu-l-misk: immā an yuḥdhiyak, wa-immā an tabtāʿa minh, wa-immā an tajida minhu rīḥan ṭayyibah. Wa-nāfikhu-l-kīr: immā an yuḥriqa thiyābak, wa-immā an tajida rīḥan khabīthah

مَثَلُ الجَلِيسِ الصَّالِحِ وَالسَّوْءِ
Mathalu-l-jalīsi-ṣ-ṣāliḥi wa-s-sawʾ
Two kinds of companion are set side by side for comparison.
الجَلِيسِ — root ج ل س. A jalīs is the person you sit beside. The word is about proximity, which is exactly what the hadith is warning about.
كَحَامِلِ المِسْكِ وَنَافِخِ الكِيرِ
ka-ḥāmili-l-miski wa-nāfikhi-l-kīr
One carries perfume; the other works a blacksmith's fire.
الكِيرِ — root ك ي ر. The author describes the kīr: a clay structure in which the blacksmith blows up his fire. Both men are pictured at their trade, not idle.
فَحَامِلُ المِسْكِ: إِمَّا أَنْ يُحْذِيَكَ، وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَبْتَاعَ مِنْهُ
Fa-ḥāmilu-l-misk: immā an yuḥdhiyak, wa-immā an tabtāʿa minh
From the musk-seller you gain, whether he gives or you pay.
يُحْذِيَكَ — root ح ذ و. The author glosses yuḥdhiyak: he gives you some for nothing. And tabtāʿa, root ب ي ع, he glosses as 'you buy'.
وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَجِدَ مِنْهُ رِيحاً طَيِّبَةً
wa-immā an tajida minhu rīḥan ṭayyibah
Even if you gain nothing at all, the good scent still reaches you.
رِيحاً — root ر و ح. Rīḥ is the scent carried on air. Nearness alone is enough for this third benefit; you need do nothing.
وَنَافِخُ الكِيرِ: إِمَّا أَنْ يُحْرِقَ ثِيَابَكَ
Wa-nāfikhu-l-kīr: immā an yuḥriqa thiyābak
The other man's trade can cost you outright.
يُحْرِقَ — root ح ر ق. Iḥrāq is burning. The harm is not only in what he says to you but in what sitting there does to you.
وَإِمَّا أَنْ تَجِدَ رِيحاً خَبِيثَةً
wa-immā an tajida rīḥan khabīthah
And at the least, you leave carrying his smoke.
خَبِيثَةً — root خ ب ث. Khabīth is foul, the opposite of ṭayyib in the earlier line. Note there is no third option here: nothing good comes of that seat.

مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses
الكِيرِالكِيرُ: بِنَاءٌ مِنْ طِينٍ، يُوقِدُ فِيهِ الحَدَّادُ النَّارَ.
al-kīr — the blacksmith's forgeAl-kīr: a structure of clay in which the blacksmith kindles the fire.
يُحْذِيَكَأَيْ: يُعْطِيَكَ مَجَاناً.
yuḥdhiyaka — he gives you a giftThat is: he gives you [something] free of charge.
تَبْتَاعَأَيْ: تَشْتَرِيَ.
tabtāʿa — you buyThat is: you purchase.

Chapter 111 — Praising a Man to His Face

Book p.222 · العِشْرَةُ — Keeping Company · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
أَثْنَى رَجُلٌ عَلَى رَجُلٍ عِنْدَ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ فَقَالَA man praised another man in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ, so he said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«وَيْلَكَ، قَطَعْتَ عُنُقَ صَاحِبِكَ، قَطَعْتَ عُنُقَ صَاحِبِكَ - مِرَاراً -. مَنْ كَانَ مِنْكُمْ مَادِحاً أَخَاهُ لَا مَحَالَةَ؛ فَلْيَقُلْ: أَحْسِبُ فُلَاناً وَاللَّهُ حَسِيبُهُ، وَلَا أُزَكِّي عَلَى اللَّهِ أَحَداً، أَحْسِبُهُ كَذَا وَكَذَا - إِنْ كَانَ يَعْلَمُ ذَلِكَ مِنْهُ -»

مِرَاراًseveral times

الكِتَاب ✎Book's words, our extraction
قُلْSay this if there is no way to avoid praising someone.
أَحْسِبُ فُلَاناً وَاللَّهُ حَسِيبُهُ، وَلَا أُزَكِّي عَلَى اللَّهِ أَحَداً، أَحْسِبُهُ كَذَا وَكَذَا
✎Added by us

“Woe to you! You have cut your companion's neck, you have cut your companion's neck” (said several times). “Whoever among you must praise his brother, let him say: ‘I reckon so-and-so, and Allāh is the one who reckons him, and I do not declare anyone pure before Allāh. I reckon him to be such and such,’ if he knows that of him.”

EstablishesPraise to a man's face is dangerous; if unavoidable, say only what you know and leave judgement to Allāh.

A man praised another in his hearing, and the Prophet ﷺ answered with alarm, twice over.
وَيْلَكَ — root و ي ل. Waylaka is a cry of ruin. The book explains it here as: you have destroyed him.

Man kāna minkum mādiḥan akhāhu lā maḥālah; fa-l-yaqul
If a situation leaves no way out of praising someone, there is a form of words for it.
مَحَالَةَ — root ح و ل. Lā maḥālah is 'no way around it'. The book explains it as a case where praising him cannot be avoided.

He states his own estimate and hands the accounting over to Allāh.
حَسِيبُهُ — root ح س ب. The book explains: I think him to be so, and Allāh is the one who takes charge of his reckoning.

wa-lā uzakkī ʿala-llāhi aḥadan
He refuses to certify anyone's standing with Allāh.
أُزَكِّي — root ز ك و. To declare someone pure. The book explains: I do not swear to anyone's godfearing before Allāh.
أَحْسِبُهُ كَذَا وَكَذَا - إِنْ كَانَ يَعْلَمُ ذَلِكَ مِنْهُ -
aḥsibuhu kadhā wa-kadhā (in kāna yaʿlamu dhālika minh)
Even the estimate is limited to what he has actually seen of the man.
يَعْلَمُ — root ع ل م. The permission runs only as far as his knowledge. Beyond that he has nothing to say.

✎Added by us

“Whoever believes in Allāh and the Last Day, let him say something good, or let him keep silent.”

EstablishesFaith leaves the tongue two options: say something good, or say nothing.

Man kāna yuʾminu bi-llāhi wa-l-yawmi-l-ākhir; fa-l-yaqul khayran, aw li-yaṣmut

مَنْwhoever
كَانَis

The instruction is tied to belief itself, not to manners or taste.
يُؤْمِنُ — root ء م ن. The present tense makes it ongoing belief. What follows is put forward as a test of it.

Speech is permitted when what is said is good.
خَيْراً — root خ ي ر. Khayran is indefinite: any good at all counts. The condition is on the content, not the length.

The alternative is silence, offered as a real option rather than a defeat.
لِيَصْمُتْ — root ص م ت. Ṣamt is deliberate silence, holding the tongue on purpose.

قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«عَلَيْكُمْ بِالصِّدْقِ؛ فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى البِرِّ. وَإِنَّ البِرَّ يَهْدِي إِلَى الجَنَّةِ. وَمَا يَزَالُ الرَّجُلُ يَصْدُقُ وَيَتَحَرَّى الصِّدْقَ حَتَّى يُكْتَبَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ صِدِّيقاً. وَإِيَّاكُمْ وَالكَذِبَ؛ فَإِنَّ الكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الفُجُورِ. وَإِنَّ الفُجُورَ يَهْدِي إِلَى النَّارِ. وَمَا يَزَالُ الرَّجُلُ يَكْذِبُ وَيَتَحَرَّى الكَذِبَ حَتَّى يُكْتَبَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَذَّاباً»

✎Added by us

“Hold to truthfulness, for truthfulness leads to righteousness, and righteousness leads to Paradise. A man keeps telling the truth and seeking out the truth until he is written down with Allāh as one who is utterly truthful. And beware of lying, for lying leads to corruption, and corruption leads to the Fire. A man keeps lying and seeking out lies until he is written down with Allāh as a liar.”

EstablishesTruthfulness leads to Paradise and lying leads to the Fire; the habit hardens into a name recorded with Allāh.

ʿAlaykum bi-ṣ-ṣidq; fa-inna-ṣ-ṣidqa yahdī ilā-l-birr. Wa-inna-l-birra yahdī ilā-l-jannah. Wa-mā yazālu-r-rajulu yaṣduqu wa-yataḥarrā-ṣ-ṣidqa ḥattā yuktaba ʿinda-llāhi ṣiddīqan. Wa-iyyākum wa-l-kadhib; fa-inna-l-kadhiba yahdī ilā-l-fujūr. Wa-inna-l-fujūra yahdī ilā-n-nār. Wa-mā yazālu-r-rajulu yakdhibu wa-yataḥarrā-l-kadhiba ḥattā yuktaba ʿinda-llāhi kadhdhāban

ʿAlaykum bi-ṣ-ṣidq
A command in the shortest possible form: stay with the truth.
بِالصِّدْقِ — root ص د ق. Ṣidq is speech that matches what is really so. The ʿalaykum bi- construction works as an imperative.
فَإِنَّ الصِّدْقَ يَهْدِي إِلَى البِرِّ. وَإِنَّ البِرَّ يَهْدِي إِلَى الجَنَّةِ.
fa-inna-ṣ-ṣidqa yahdī ilā-l-birr. Wa-inna-l-birra yahdī ilā-l-jannah
Two steps are traced: truth to righteousness, righteousness to Paradise.
البِرِّ — root ب ر ر. The book explains: birr is a name that gathers all good under it.
وَمَا يَزَالُ الرَّجُلُ يَصْدُقُ وَيَتَحَرَّى الصِّدْقَ حَتَّى يُكْتَبَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ صِدِّيقاً.
Wa-mā yazālu-r-rajulu yaṣduqu wa-yataḥarrā-ṣ-ṣidqa ḥattā yuktaba ʿinda-llāhi ṣiddīqan
Truth told again and again earns a title that is written into the record.
وَيَتَحَرَّى — root ح ر ي. The book explains: he aims at it and takes care over it. Truth is chosen on purpose, not stumbled on.
وَإِيَّاكُمْ وَالكَذِبَ؛
Wa-iyyākum wa-l-kadhib
The warning against the opposite is put as sharply as the command was.
وَالكَذِبَ — root ك ذ ب. Kadhib is speech that does not match what is really so, the exact reverse of ṣidq.
فَإِنَّ الكَذِبَ يَهْدِي إِلَى الفُجُورِ. وَإِنَّ الفُجُورَ يَهْدِي إِلَى النَّارِ.
fa-inna-l-kadhiba yahdī ilā-l-fujūr. Wa-inna-l-fujūra yahdī ilā-n-nār
The same two steps, running the other way.
الفُجُورِ — root ف ج ر. The book explains: fujūr is turning off the straight road and rushing into sins.
وَمَا يَزَالُ الرَّجُلُ يَكْذِبُ وَيَتَحَرَّى الكَذِبَ حَتَّى يُكْتَبَ عِنْدَ اللَّهِ كَذَّاباً
Wa-mā yazālu-r-rajulu yakdhibu wa-yataḥarrā-l-kadhiba ḥattā yuktaba ʿinda-llāhi kadhdhāban
Lying repeated also earns a name, and that name is written down too.
كَذَّاباً — root ك ذ ب. The intensive form: not a man who lied once, but a man whose trade is lying.

Chapter 117 — The Good Word

Book p.232 · اللِّسَانُ — The Tongue · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«الكَلِمَةُ الطَّيِّبَةُ صَدَقَةٌ»

✎Added by us

“A good word is charity.”

EstablishesA good word counts as charity, so speech itself is a way of giving.

Al-kalimatu-ṭ-ṭayyibatu ṣadaqah

الكَلِمَةُthe word
الطَّيِّبَةُthe good
صَدَقَةٌis charity
الكَلِمَةُ الطَّيِّبَةُ
Al-kalimatu-ṭ-ṭayyibah
One word, described only as good.
الطَّيِّبَةُ — root ط ي ب. Ṭayyib is what is wholesome and pleasant, the opposite of foul. It covers kindness, truth and dhikr alike.
صَدَقَةٌ
ṣadaqah
It is entered in the books the way money given away is entered.
صَدَقَةٌ — root ص د ق. The same root as ṣidq. A ṣadaqah shows the giver is sincere, and this one costs nothing but the tongue.

«سِبَابُ المُسْلِمِ فُسُوقٌ، وَقِتَالُهُ كُفْرٌ»

✎Added by us

“Reviling a Muslim is disobedience, and fighting him is disbelief.”

EstablishesReviling a Muslim is named disobedience, and fighting him is named disbelief.

Sibābu-l-muslimi fusūq, wa-qitāluhu kufr

Abuse is not treated as a small fault. It is given a name.

The step beyond abuse is named with the heaviest word available.
كُفْرٌ — root ك ف ر. Kufr is covering over and denying. Placing the word here shows how far fighting a Muslim stands from faith.

عَنْ عَائِشَةَ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَا قَالَتْʿĀʾishah (may Allāh be pleased with her) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«قُلْتُ لِلنَّبِيِّ ﷺ: حَسْبُكَ مِنْ صَفِيَّةَ كَذَا وَكَذَا - تَعْنِي: قَصِيرَةً -. فَقَالَ: لَقَدْ قُلْتِ كَلِمَةً لَوْ مُزِجَتْ بِمَاءِ البَحْرِ لَمَزَجَتْهُ»

✎Added by us

I said to the Prophet ﷺ, “Enough about Ṣafiyyah: she is such and such,” meaning that she was short. He said, “You have said a word which, if it were mixed with the water of the sea, would change it.”

EstablishesEven a brief remark about a person's body is backbiting, and heavy enough to change the sea.

Qultu li-n-Nabiyyi ﷺ
ʿĀʾishah reports her own words, spoken in the Prophet's hearing.
قُلْتُ — root ق و ل. She narrates this against herself, which is how the lesson reached us at all.
حَسْبُكَ مِنْ صَفِيَّةَ كَذَا وَكَذَا - تَعْنِي: قَصِيرَةً -.
Ḥasbuka min Ṣafiyyata kadhā wa-kadhā (taʿnī: qaṣīratan)
One passing remark about another wife's height.
حَسْبُكَ — root ح س ب. Ḥasbuka is 'that is enough for you', here a dismissive summing-up of a whole person.
فَقَالَ: لَقَدْ قُلْتِ كَلِمَةً
Fa-qāla: La-qad qulti kalimatan
He does not argue about whether the remark was accurate. He weighs it.
كَلِمَةً — root ك ل م. Kalimah is one word. The size of the speech and the size of the sin are not the same size.
لَوْ مُزِجَتْ بِمَاءِ البَحْرِ لَمَزَجَتْهُ
law muzijat bi-māʾi-l-baḥri la-mazajath
Dropped into the sea, this one word would spoil the whole of it.
مُزِجَتْ — root م ز ج. The book explains muzijat as 'was mixed' and la-mazajathu as 'would change it'. A little in a lot, and the lot turns.

قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَمَّا عُرِجَ بِي؛ مَرَرْتُ بِقَوْمٍ لَهُمْ أَظْفَارٌ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ، يَخْمِشُونَ وُجُوهَهُمْ وَصُدُورَهُمْ. فَقُلْتُ: مَنْ هَؤُلَاءِ يَا جِبْرِيلُ؟ قَالَ: هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ يَأْكُلُونَ لُحُومَ النَّاسِ، وَيَقَعُونَ فِي أَعْرَاضِهِمْ»

✎Added by us

“When I was taken up, I passed by a people who had nails of copper, tearing at their faces and their chests. I said, ‘Who are these, Jibrīl?’ He said, ‘These are the ones who eat the flesh of people and fall upon their honour.’”

EstablishesBackbiting is shown as eating people's flesh, and its punishment is tearing one's own face and chest.

Lammā ʿurija bī; marartu bi-qawmin lahum aẓfārun min nuḥās, yakhmishūna wujūhahum wa-ṣudūrahum. Fa-qultu: Man hāʾulāʾi yā Jibrīl? Qāla: Hāʾulāʾi-lladhīna yaʾkulūna luḥūma-n-nās, wa-yaqaʿūna fī aʿrāḍihim

The answer names the sin twice over: eating flesh, and falling on reputations.
لُحُومَ — root ل ح م. The book explains 'eating people's flesh' as backbiting them. What felt like talk is shown as feeding on a body.

Book p.237 · اللِّسَانُ — The Tongue · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«وَيْلٌ لِلَّذِي يُحَدِّثُ فَيَكْذِبُ؛ لِيُضْحِكَ بِهِ القَوْمَ، وَيْلٌ لَهُ، وَيْلٌ لَهُ»

✎Added by us

“Woe to the one who tells a story and lies in it, to make the gathering laugh. Woe to him, woe to him.”

EstablishesA lie told to make people laugh brings woe on the teller, said three times over.

وَيْلٌwoe

A man is telling a story and putting falsehood into it.
يُحَدِّثُ — root ح د ث. Ḥaddatha is to relate a piece of news or a story. The setting is ordinary conversation, not testimony.
لِيُضْحِكَ بِهِ القَوْمَ،
li-yuḍḥika bihi-l-qawm
His purpose is the laugh, and the purpose does not excuse the lie.
لِيُضْحِكَ — root ض ح ك. The lām gives his aim: to make others laugh. The aim is stated plainly, then the woe follows anyway.
وَيْلٌ لَهُ، وَيْلٌ لَهُ
waylun lah, waylun lah
The cry is repeated, so it stands three times in one short sentence.
وَيْلٌ — root و ي ل. Wayl is a cry of ruin. Repetition is how the warning is pressed rather than argued.

تَوَاضَعَ — root و ض ع. Tawāḍaʿa is to set yourself down on purpose. The lām in li-llāh fixes the motive: for Allāh, not for effect.

The sentence opens with the greater debt: thanks owed to Allāh.

Failing the smaller debt means the greater one has not been paid either.

Chapter 128 — Envy

Book p.248 · صِفَاتٌ مَذْمُومَةٌ — Blameworthy Traits · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا تَبَاغَضُوا، وَلَا تَحَاسَدُوا، وَلَا تَدَابَرُوا، وَكُونُوا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ إِخْوَاناً»

✎Added by us

“Do not hate one another, do not envy one another, do not turn your backs on one another. And be brothers, servants of Allāh.”

EstablishesMutual hatred, envy, and cutting each other off are forbidden; Muslims are ordered to live as brothers.

Lā tabāghaḍū, wa lā taḥāsadū, wa lā tadābarū, wa kūnū ʿibāda-llāhi ikhwānā

لَاdo not
تَبَاغَضُواhate one another

Lā tabāghaḍū, wa lā taḥāsadū
Two things are banned before anything is asked: hatred, then envy.
تَحَاسَدُوا — root ح س د. Ḥasad is wanting what another has and wanting him to lose it. The verb form is reciprocal, so neither side may start.
وَلَا تَدَابَرُوا
wa lā tadābarū
The third ban is on the silent break in relations.
تَدَابَرُوا — root د ب ر. Dubur is the back, so tadābur is turning backs on each other. The author glosses it: do not cut each other off.
وَكُونُوا عِبَادَ اللَّهِ إِخْوَاناً
wa kūnū ʿibāda-llāhi ikhwānā
The three bans are replaced with one instruction: be brothers.
إِخْوَاناً — root أ خ و. Ikhwān is the plural of akh, brother. It names the relation that is meant to stand where hatred and envy were.

Chapter 129 — Suspicion

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِيَّاكُمْ وَالظَّنَّ؛ فَإِنَّ الظَّنَّ أَكْذَبُ الحَدِيثِ»

✎Added by us

“Beware of suspicion, for suspicion is the most false of speech.”

EstablishesBad suspicion of others is to be avoided; it is inner speech, and the falsest speech of all.

Iyyākum wa-ẓ-ẓann; fa-inna-ẓ-ẓanna akdhabu-l-ḥadīth

إِيَّاكُمْbeware

Iyyākum wa-ẓ-ẓann
This is a warning to keep clear of something, not a suggestion.
وَالظَّنَّ — root ظ ن ن. Ẓann is a thought held without proof. The author specifies which kind is meant: beware of bad suspicion.
فَإِنَّ الظَّنَّ أَكْذَبُ الحَدِيثِ
fa-inna-ẓ-ẓanna akdhabu-l-ḥadīth
The reason is given at once: nothing a person tells himself is less reliable.
أَكْذَبُ — root ك ذ ب. Akdhab is the superlative of kādhib, false. The author explains it: ẓann is the speech of the self, and the self's speech is falser than a man's spoken word, because Shayṭān casts it there.

akdhab al-ḥadīth — the most lying of speechHe described suspicion as “the most lying of speech” because suspicion is the speech of the soul, whereas speaking is the speech of the man; and the speech of the soul is more lying than the speech of the man, because the speech of the soul comes about by Satan's casting [it] into the soul of the man.

“It is not lawful for a Muslim to shun his brother beyond three nights: they meet, and this one turns away, and that one turns away. The better of the two is the one who begins with the greeting.”

Lā yaḥillu li-muslimin an yahjura akhāhu fawqa thalāthi layāl
A limit is set on estrangement: three nights, and no more.
يَهْجُرَ — root ه ج ر. Hajr is abandonment. The author glosses tahājur as cutting off and turning away from one another.

مُرُوطَهُنَّtheir waist-wraps

بِهَاwith them
يَرْحَمُ اللَّهُ نِسَاءَ المُهَاجِرَاتِ الأُوَلَ
Yarḥamu-llāhu nisāʾa-l-muhājirāti-l-uwal
ʿĀʾishah begins by praying for the earliest women who left Makkah for Madīnah.
المُهَاجِرَاتِ — root ه ج ر. Muhājirāt are the women who made the hijrah. Al-uwal marks these as the first of them, the ones she is holding up as an example.
لَمَّا أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ: ﴿وَلْيَضْرِبْنَ بِخُمُرِهِنَّ عَلَىٰ جُيُوبِهِنَّ﴾
lammā anzala-llāhu: Wa-l-yaḍribna bi-khumurihinna ʿalā juyūbihinn
A verse came down telling believing women to bring their head-coverings down over the opening of the garment.
بِخُمُرِهِنَّ — root خ م ر. The author defines the khimār as what the head and the face are covered with, and the jayb as the head-opening of the garment: the khimār on the head is lowered to it, so head, face, throat and chest are covered together.
شَقَّقْنَ مُرُوطَهُنَّ، فَاخْتَمَرْنَ بِهَا
shaqqaqna murūṭahunna, fa-khtamarna bihā
They cut up cloth they already owned and made coverings out of it on the spot.
مُرُوطَهُنَّ — root م ر ط. The author explains murūṭ as the plural of mirṭ: the izār, a length of cloth wrapped round the lower half of the body.

مِنْ حَاشِيَةِ الكِتَابThe author's own footnote glosses

al-khimār — the head coveringAl-khimār: that with which the head and the face are covered.
الجَيْبُالجَيْبُ: مَدْخَلُ الرَّأْسِ مِنَ الثَّوْبِ؛ أَيْ: لِيُنْزِلْنَ الخِمَارَ الَّذِي عَلَى الرَّأْسِ إِلَى مَدْخَلِ الرَّأْسِ مِنَ الثَّوْبِ؛ لِيَتَغَطَّى بِذَلِكَ الرَّأْسُ مَعَ الوَجْهِ وَالنَّحْرِ وَالصَّدْرِ

المُرُوطُالمُرُوطُ: جَمْعُ مِرْطٍ، وَهُوَ: الإِزَارُ، وَهُوَ القِطْعَةُ مِنَ القُمَاشِ تُلَفُّ عَلَى النِّصْفِ الأَسْفَلِ مِنَ الجَسَدِ

Chapter 136 — A Woman Travelling Without a Maḥram Is Forbidden

Book p.258 · المَرْأَةُ — Women · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا تُسَافِرِ المَرْأَةُ إِلَّا مَعَ ذِي مَحْرَمٍ. وَلَا يَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهَا رَجُلٌ إِلَّا وَمَعَهَا مَحْرَمٌ. فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ فِي جَيْشِ كَذَا وَكَذَا، وَامْرَأَتِي تُرِيدُ الحَجَّ. فَقَالَ: اخْرُجْ مَعَهَا»

✎Added by us

“A woman is not to travel except with a maḥram, and no man is to come in upon her unless a maḥram is with her.” A man said, “Messenger of Allāh, I want to go out with such and such an army, and my wife wants to make Ḥajj.” He said, “Go out with her.”

EstablishesA woman travels only with a maḥram; a man is told to accompany his wife's Ḥajj rather than join the campaign.

Lā tusāfiri-l-marʾatu illā maʿa dhī maḥram. Wa lā yadkhulu ʿalayhā rajulun illā wa maʿahā maḥram. Fa-qāla rajul: Yā Rasūla-llāh, innī urīdu an akhruja fī jayshi kadhā wa kadhā, wa-mraʾatī turīdu-l-ḥajj. Fa-qāla: Ukhruj maʿahā

إِلَّاexcept

تُرِيدُwants
الحَجَّthe Ḥajj
فَقَالَso he said
اخْرُجْgo out
مَعَهَاwith her
لَا تُسَافِرِ المَرْأَةُ إِلَّا مَعَ ذِي مَحْرَمٍ
Lā tusāfiri-l-marʾatu illā maʿa dhī maḥram
Travel is permitted to her with a maḥram and not otherwise.
مَحْرَمٍ — root ح ر م. A maḥram is a relative she may never marry: father, brother, son, uncle and the like. The word comes from what is made forbidden.
وَلَا يَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهَا رَجُلٌ إِلَّا وَمَعَهَا مَحْرَمٌ
wa lā yadkhulu ʿalayhā rajulun illā wa maʿahā maḥram
The same condition governs a man coming in to where she is.
يَدْخُلُ — root د خ ل. Yadkhulu ʿalayhā is to come in upon her. The condition is the maḥram's presence, stated without reference to the man's intention.
فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، إِنِّي أُرِيدُ أَنْ أَخْرُجَ فِي جَيْشِ كَذَا وَكَذَا، وَامْرَأَتِي تُرِيدُ الحَجَّ
Fa-qāla rajul: Yā Rasūla-llāh, innī urīdu an akhruja fī jayshi kadhā wa kadhā, wa-mraʾatī turīdu-l-ḥajj
A man brings a real clash: he is due to go on campaign, and his wife wants to make Ḥajj.
جَيْشِ — root ج ي ش. Jaysh is an army. Kadhā wa kadhā stands in for a name the narrator did not preserve, so the campaign is left unidentified.
فَقَالَ: اخْرُجْ مَعَهَا
Fa-qāla: Ukhruj maʿahā
The answer is three words: go with your wife.
اخْرُجْ — root خ ر ج. Ukhruj is a command, go out. The clash is resolved in favour of accompanying her, and no other option is offered.

Chapter 137 — The Husband's Right Over His Wife

Book p.259 · المَرْأَةُ — Women · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَوْ كُنْتُ آمِراً أَحَداً أَنْ يَسْجُدَ لِأَحَدٍ، لَأَمَرْتُ المَرْأَةَ أَنْ تَسْجُدَ لِزَوْجِهَا»

✎Added by us

“Were I to order anyone to prostrate to anyone, I would have ordered the woman to prostrate to her husband.”

EstablishesThe husband's right is so great that prostration to him would be ordered, were prostration to any human being allowed.

Law kuntu āmiran aḥadan an yasjuda li-aḥad, la-amartu-l-marʾata an tasjuda li-zawjihā

لَوْwere
كُنْتُI to be

لِزَوْجِهَاto her husband
لَوْ كُنْتُ آمِراً أَحَداً أَنْ يَسْجُدَ لِأَحَدٍ
Law kuntu āmiran aḥadan an yasjuda li-aḥad
The sentence opens with a case that does not exist: no human being is ever to be prostrated to.
آمِراً — root أ م ر. Āmir is the active participle, one who orders. Law sets up a condition understood not to hold, so the order is never actually given.
لَأَمَرْتُ المَرْأَةَ
la-amartu-l-marʾata
If it were ever going to be ordered, this is who would be ordered.
لَأَمَرْتُ — root أ م ر. La-amartu is the answer to law: I would have ordered. The lām ties it back to the case just supposed.
أَنْ تَسْجُدَ لِزَوْجِهَا
an tasjuda li-zawjihā
The one it would be directed to is her husband.
لِزَوْجِهَا — root ز و ج. Zawj is a spouse; here it means the husband. The lām marks the one the prostration would be aimed at.

Book p.260 · المَرْأَةُ — Women · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ جَرِيرُ بْنُ عَبْدِ اللَّهِ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُJarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh (may Allāh be pleased with him) said

«سَأَلْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ عَنْ نَظَرِ الفُجَاءَةِ؟ فَأَمَرَنِي أَنْ أَصْرِفَ بَصَرِي»

✎Added by us

Jarīr ibn ʿAbd Allāh, may Allāh be pleased with him, said: “I asked the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ about the sudden glance, and he ordered me to turn my gaze away.”

EstablishesA glance that falls on a woman unintentionally must be turned away at once, by the Prophet's own instruction.

Saʾaltu Rasūla-llāhi ﷺ ʿan naẓari-l-fujāʾah; fa-amaranī an aṣrifa baṣarī

سَأَلْتُI asked

عَنْabout
نَظَرِthe glance of
الفُجَاءَةِsuddenness
فَأَمَرَنِيso he ordered me
أَنْto

سَأَلْتُ رَسُولَ اللَّهِ ﷺ عَنْ نَظَرِ الفُجَاءَةِ
Saʾaltu Rasūla-llāhi ﷺ ʿan naẓari-l-fujāʾah
Jarīr asks about the case where the eye lands on something before he has chosen to look.
الفُجَاءَةِ — root ف ج أ. Fujāʾah is suddenness. The author defines naẓar al-fujāʾah as his gaze falling on a woman who is not his maḥram, without his meaning it.
فَأَمَرَنِي أَنْ أَصْرِفَ بَصَرِي
fa-amaranī an aṣrifa baṣarī
The instruction concerns what he does next, not the glance itself.
أَصْرِفَ — root ص ر ف. Ṣarafa is to turn something away or divert it. The order is to move the gaze off, immediately, rather than let it settle.

naẓar al-fujāʾah — the sudden glanceNaẓar al-fujāʾah: that his gaze falls upon a woman not related to him without intending it.

Chapter 139 — Entering Upon Women Is Forbidden

Book p.261 · المَرْأَةُ — Women · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِيَّاكُمْ وَالدُّخُولَ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ. فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الأَنْصَارِ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، أَفَرَأَيْتَ الحَمْوَ؟ قَالَ: الحَمْوُ المَوْتُ»

✎Added by us

“Beware of entering upon women.” A man from the Anṣār said, “Messenger of Allāh, what about the husband's relative?” He said, “The husband's relative is death.”

EstablishesEntering upon women who are not maḥram is forbidden, and the husband's male relatives are singled out as most dangerous.

Iyyākum wa-d-dukhūla ʿalā-n-nisāʾ. Fa-qāla rajulun mina-l-Anṣār: Yā Rasūla-llāh, a-fa-raʾayta-l-ḥamw? Qāla: Al-ḥamwu-l-mawt

عَلَىupon

Iyyākum wa-d-dukhūla ʿalā-n-nisāʾ
A warning to keep away from going in to women.
وَالدُّخُولَ — root د خ ل. Dukhūl is entering. The author specifies which women: those forbidden to him, and the manner meant is being alone with them or their being uncovered.
فَقَالَ رَجُلٌ مِنَ الأَنْصَارِ: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، أَفَرَأَيْتَ الحَمْوَ
Fa-qāla rajulun mina-l-Anṣār: Yā Rasūla-llāh, a-fa-raʾayta-l-ḥamw
A man asks about the case people assume is exempt: the husband's own family.
الحَمْوَ — root ح م و. The author defines ḥamw as the husband's brother, and others among the husband's relatives such as a cousin.
قَالَ: الحَمْوُ المَوْتُ

The answer is two words, with no verb between them.
المَوْتُ — root م و ت. Mawt is death. The author reads the sentence as: his entering is ruinous like death, meaning the danger in it is severe.

Chapter 140 — The Prohibition of Shaking Hands with Women Who Are Not Close Relatives

Book p.262 · المَرْأَةُ — Women · 2 entries in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«إِنِّي لَا أُصَافِحُ النِّسَاءَ»

✎Added by us

“Indeed, I do not shake hands with women.”

EstablishesThe book takes the Prophet's own refusal as the rule: no handshake with women outside close kin.

Innī lā uṣāfiḥu-n-nisāʾ

إِنِّيindeed I
لَاdo not
أُصَافِحُshake hands with
النِّسَاءَwomen
إِنِّي لَا أُصَافِحُ
Innī lā uṣāfiḥu
He describes his own standing practice, not a decision made for one occasion.
أُصَافِحُ — root ص ف ح, Form III. Muṣāfaḥah is palm laid against palm, the ordinary greeting. The verb is present tense, so the refusal is continuous.
النِّسَاءَ
-n-nisāʾ
The object is women as a class, so no particular case is being singled out.
النِّسَاءَ — root ن س و. An-nisāʾ is the plural of woman carrying the definite article, which makes it general.

رَوَاهُ أَحْمَدُReported by Aḥmad

٢
قَالَتْ عَائِشَةُ رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهَاʿĀʾishah (may Allāh be pleased with her) said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«وَاللَّهِ، مَا مَسَّتْ يَدُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ يَدَ امْرَأَةٍ قَطُّ»

✎Added by us

ʿĀʾishah (may Allāh be pleased with her) said: “By Allāh, the hand of the Messenger of Allāh ﷺ never touched the hand of a woman.”

EstablishesThe book cites ʿĀʾishah to show the practice held for a lifetime: his hand never touched a woman's hand.

Wa-llāhi, mā massat yadu Rasūli-llāhi ﷺ yada imraʾatin qaṭṭ

وَاللَّهِby Allāh
مَاnever
مَسَّتْtouched
يَدُthe hand of
رَسُولِ اللَّهِthe Messenger of Allāh
يَدَthe hand of
امْرَأَةٍa woman
قَطُّat any time
وَاللَّهِ، مَا
Wa-llāhi, mā
She swears an oath first, then begins a flat denial.
وَاللَّهِ — root أ ل ه with the oath particle wāw. Swearing by Allāh marks what follows as exact reporting, not an impression.
مَسَّتْ يَدُ رَسُولِ اللَّهِ ﷺ يَدَ
massat yadu Rasūli-llāhi ﷺ yada
Hand and hand are named on both sides, so what is denied is the contact itself.
مَسَّتْ — root م س س. Massa is bare touching, the lightest kind of contact there is. Nothing heavier has to be imagined for the report to hold.
امْرَأَةٍ قَطُّ
imraʾatin qaṭṭ
An indefinite 'a woman' with qaṭṭ makes it total: no woman, on no occasion.
قَطُّ — root ق ط ط. Qaṭṭ shuts off all past time, 'not once ever'. Arabic uses it only after a negative.

قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«لَا يَخْلُوَنَّ رَجُلٌ بِامْرَأَةٍ لَا تَحِلُّ لَهُ؛ فَإِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ ثَالِثُهُمَا»

✎Added by us

“Let no man be alone with a woman who is not lawful for him, for Satan is the third of them.”

EstablishesA man is not to be alone with a woman not lawful to him; the reason given is Satan's presence.

Lā yakhluwanna rajulun bi-imraʾatin lā taḥillu lah; fa-inna-sh-shayṭāna thālithuhumā

لَاlet not
يَخْلُوَنَّbe alone
رَجُلٌa man
بِامْرَأَةٍwith a woman
لَاnot
تَحِلُّshe is lawful
لَهُfor him
فَإِنَّfor indeed
الشَّيْطَانَSatan
ثَالِثُهُمَاis the third of the two
لَا يَخْلُوَنَّ رَجُلٌ بِامْرَأَةٍ
Lā yakhluwanna rajulun bi-imraʾatin
A prohibition in its strongest form: this is not to happen at all.
يَخْلُوَنَّ — root خ ل و. Khalwah is being shut away with someone where no one else can come in. The doubled nūn on the verb makes the ban emphatic.
لَا تَحِلُّ لَهُ؛
lā taḥillu lah
The ruling is limited to women he is not permitted to marry; a wife and close kin fall outside it.
تَحِلُّ — root ح ل ل. Ḥalāl is what has been untied and allowed. The line is drawn at lawfulness, not at what either of them intends.
فَإِنَّ الشَّيْطَانَ ثَالِثُهُمَا
fa-inna-sh-shayṭāna thālithuhumā
The reason is stated: someone else is already present whom neither of them counted.
ثَالِثُهُمَا — root ث ل ث. Thālith simply means 'third'. Two who believe they are alone are being counted as three.

رَوَاهُ النَّسَائِيُّ فِي السُّنَنِ الكُبْرَىReported by al-Nasāʾī in al-Sunan al-Kubrā

Chapter 142 — Loving to Meet Allāh

Book p.266 · لِقَاءُ اللَّهِ ﷻ — Meeting Allāh · 1 entry in the printed text.

١
قَالَ النَّبِيُّ ﷺThe Prophet ﷺ said
الكِتَابFrom the book

«مَنْ أَحَبَّ لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ أَحَبَّ اللَّهُ لِقَاءَهُ. وَمَنْ كَرِهَ لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ كَرِهَ اللَّهُ لِقَاءَهُ»

✎Added by us

“Whoever loves to meet Allāh, Allāh loves to meet him. And whoever hates to meet Allāh, Allāh hates to meet him.”

EstablishesThe book ends on the heart's disposition: loving to meet Allāh is answered by Allāh loving to meet the servant.

Man aḥabba liqāʾa-llāhi aḥabba-llāhu liqāʾah. Wa-man kariha liqāʾa-llāhi kariha-llāhu liqāʾah

مَنْwhoever
أَحَبَّloves
لِقَاءَthe meeting with
اللَّهِAllāh
أَحَبَّloves
اللَّهُAllāh
لِقَاءَهُmeeting him
وَمَنْand whoever
كَرِهَhates
لِقَاءَthe meeting with
اللَّهِAllāh
كَرِهَhates
اللَّهُAllāh
لِقَاءَهُmeeting him
مَنْ أَحَبَّ لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ
Man aḥabba liqāʾa-llāhi
The condition is a love in the servant, and it is placed first.
أَحَبَّ — root ح ب ب, Form IV. Aḥabba is to hold a thing dear and want it. What is wanted is the meeting, not the dying that opens onto it.
أَحَبَّ اللَّهُ لِقَاءَهُ.
aḥabba-llāhu liqāʾah
The same verb returns with Allāh as its subject, so the love is answered in kind.
لِقَاءَهُ — root ل ق ي. Liqāʾ is two parties meeting, not one arriving. The ending -hu makes the servant the one who is met.
وَمَنْ كَرِهَ لِقَاءَ اللَّهِ
wa-man kariha liqāʾa-llāhi
The other side is set out in exactly the same shape, with one word changed.
كَرِهَ — root ك ر ه. Kariha is to find something hateful and pull away from it. It names a settled aversion, not the natural fear of death.
كَرِهَ اللَّهُ لِقَاءَهُ
kariha-llāhu liqāʾah
The book's last words hand the aversion back to the one who held it.
اللَّهُ — root أ ل ه. Allāh is the subject of both halves. What the servant brings to the meeting is what he finds waiting for him.

مُتَّفَقٌ عَلَيْهِAgreed upon (al-Bukhārī and Muslim)
